1.1: 1.1 Preface. In Hebrew, ELLEH HADDEBARIM, that is, THESE ARE THE WORDS. A bundle of myrrh is chosen for me. Myrrh is an aromatic tree that grows only five cubits high; its bark, root, leaves and everything about it are bitter. Myrrh is bitter and is applied to corpses to keep off the decay of worms. This is the old law, comprised in five books: bitter, that is, sparing no one, whence it is also signified by Marah; applied to corpses, that is, found for sinners, so that it might keep the corruption of crimes from them. Its bundle is Deuteronomy, that is, a gathering into one of many little branches. For when the law had been completed in four volumes, this fifth was added, briefly collecting into one the things said at length, and also supplying certain things omitted. It was added to them so as to satisfy the number of the law. For five is the number of the law, four of the Gospel. Hence the feeding of the five thousand in the Gospel concerns the fathers of the Old Testament; the feeding of the four thousand, the fathers of the new; for to the former earthly things were promised and given, which are subject to the five senses; to the latter the squareness, that is, the solidity, of the land of the living. This book also serves the Gospel in its name, in the order of its exposition, and in its own dignity. For in Hebrew it is called Elleh Haddebarim, that is, these words; in Greek Deuteronomion, which in Latin is the second law: not as some have said, another after the one spoken of before (whence in the earlier books it was said, The Lord spoke; but here, Moses spoke), but second, that is, repeated a second time, prefiguring by this name the Gospel, which followed the law and which none will follow. Since it also briefly collects many things and supplies some, it prefigures the form of the Gospel: for this is the abbreviated word which the Lord made upon the earth, and it supplies the imperfect things of the law; whence: I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfil it (Matthew 5). When this work is said to be so worthy that the king is ordered to carry it in his hands, it reveals the dignity of the Gospel, which was ordained in the hand of the Mediator. Since, then, it so serves the Gospel, it is rightly a bundle beloved of Christ, not so much for its own sake as because it shows the wheel in the middle of the wheel. The intention is to recapitulate what was said before, with a threefold end: that it may be committed to memory more firmly; that the usefulness of what was said may be impressed; (for what is useful ought not to be wearisome to say often, as the Apostle says in Philippians 3, nor annoying to hear;) and that the hardness of the Jews may be condemned, who did not understand things said so many times. The manner of proceeding: he first sets down a sort of prologue, in which he shows who wrote and what, etc. Next he recalls the grave offence for which they perished in the desert, so that by this fear he may rouse them to listen. Then he sets apart the cities of refuge. Then he recapitulates the things said and done, and supplies good and bad things omitted. Then he commands that this book be placed in the ark, and in the seventh year be read to all Israel at the feast of Tabernacles. Then he adds the canticle, Hear, etc., in memory of their murmuring and punishment, of obedience and reward. And afterwards the blessings of the tribes. Last, the death of Moses. These are the words, etc. The lawgiver sets down a title as a sort of prologue, in which he shows the name of the author, and what he did, and where, and when. As will be distinguished a little later in the gloss, and it ends, as some think, at: In the fortieth, etc., or further on, at: Our God, etc. But for the clarity of these things, and of what follows in the prologue, the truth of the history must be touched upon a little. From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt until they came to the plains of Moab above the Jordan, forty-two years passed, in which at various times they made forty-two encampments. When the cloud was lifted, the camp was moved, and when it stood still, they pitched and stayed in the same place until the cloud was lifted again. The first encampment was at Rameses, the last in the plains of Moab. From Rameses to Mount Sinai, over a space of forty-seven days, they made twelve encampments, and this in the first year, and there they stayed almost the whole year. There the law was given; there Genesis was written, Exodus, Numbers, and a great part of this book. Moving on from there in the second year, they came to Kadesh-barnea, and in that interval they made twenty encampments; from Kadesh-barnea they sent spies, who on returning reported that the land was good, but found the men strong and giants, and, terrified and wishing to return to the land of Egypt, they angered the Lord. They went back and wandered around Mount Seir for thirty-eight years; there they died and were laid low, murmuring. In the fortieth year they came to Kadesh-barnea, from which they went back through the desert, and in that interval they again made nine encampments. For eleven days before he came to Kadesh-barnea, Moses recapitulated the law by word alone, and from Kadesh-barnea to the plains of Moab he wished to commit that space of eleven days to writing. Behold: twelve from the first year, twenty-one from the second, nine from the rest, and so forty-two encampments. This was the cause of this book: that what had been done, briefly collected, might be held more firmly in memory; for things said briefly are easily retained. RABANUS on Deuteronomy. These are the words, etc. The beginning of Deuteronomy appears to be the title of the whole work, because it indicates the person of the author, and what he did, and the place and the time. The name of the book also shows the grace of the New Testament. For Deuteronomy is interpreted as the second law, and signifies the Gospel, which spiritually explains the sacraments of the Old Testament. Just as the book of Deuteronomy is a repetition of the four books of the law: for those contain their own causes in themselves, this one repeats them all, and also has its own sacraments. The same. These are the words. He says this of himself as of another, etc., so that no one can doubt that Moses wrote these things. He spoke. Moses is the old law, which beyond the Jordan, that is, before baptism, taught the Israelite people. For in the Jordan baptism is signified, in which Christ was baptized: in the plain wilderness, that is, in the barrenness of the carnal people, who brought forth no fruit of virtues. In the wilderness, the barrenness of the people, to whom it is said: Your house shall be left to you desolate (Matthew 23; Luke 13). Over against the sea. Because the wicked and perverse generation was unwilling to believe in the washing away of sins in the blood of Christ. Between Paran. Paran, increased; Tophel, tastelessness; Laban, whitening; Hazeroth, courts. For the people was increased in the number of men, in the teaching of the law and the prophets; but it was tasteless, because it did not have the salt of wisdom; whitened indeed by the ceremonies of the law and various cleansings, which it believed it had from the letter of the law. Rightly is it signified by courts, as one prepared by the divine Scriptures for the entrance of faith, whence many at the coming of Christ more easily received him whom they had recognized as foretold, whence Philip: We have found Jesus the son of Joseph of Nazareth, of whom Moses in the law and the prophets wrote (John 1). These four mountains signify the four Gospels, by which the Church is surrounded.
1.2: 1.2 Eleven days. The law explained through Moses in eleven days signifies the transgression of the Jewish people against the commandments of the Decalogue: the eleven days are the eleven apostles, through whom, Judas being rejected, the Gospel of Christ was preached in the world. From Horeb. Which in Hebrew is Choreb; beginning through Seir, that is, passing through the hairy people, filthy with vices, he came to Kadesh-barnea: which is interpreted changed, or chosen, or noble, signifying the literal sense of the law changed into the spiritual through the Gospel. For all things happened to them in figure, and were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages are come (1 Corinthians 10). For the law is not dissolved but fulfilled, and not one jot or one tittle shall pass until all things be fulfilled (Matthew 5).
1.3: 1.3 In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first, etc. ISIDORE, on Deuteronomy, vol. 5. Forty years, etc., until they will remain without corruption. Forty consists of ten and four, and signifies the fulfilment of the law of the Gospel, which takes place in the Church; for ten pertains to the law, four to the Gospel. In the eleventh month, etc. As in the eleventh the transgression of the law is expressed, so on the first day the lawgiver's intention to teach was watchful; for from the time the disobedient people did not fear to transgress the law, he immediately, by preaching and correcting, strove to make known the will of the Lord, and did not cease, by words and examples, to draw or urge them to better things.
1.4: 1.4 After he had struck Sihon, etc. It is to be noted that, the two kings of the Amorites having been slain, the law is recapitulated and the people instructed, because, once scandals are removed and the troops of vices overcome, teaching is fittingly pursued and the light of faith is worthily opened to those who desire it. We ought first to kill the vices in ourselves, and so hand on the divine commands to the peoples. Sihon king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon, etc. ISIDORE. In these kings, etc., until but staying outside, let them always persist in wicked works.
1.5: 1.5 In the land of Moab. For it was a lawless people, which did not have the spiritual law.
1.6: 1.6 The Lord our God. In the book of Numbers the departure of the children of Israel from the desert of Sinai is narrated, but the command of the Lord to Moses about that same crossing is not given; rather there is mention of the cloud that covered the tabernacle, which withdrew when it was time to set out, and went before to the place for pitching the camp. For so it is written: In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the covenant, and rested in the wilderness of Paran (Numbers 10). But it is clear that that crossing was ordered by the command of God, though it is not recorded there. Hence elsewhere in the book of Numbers, at the Lord's command they pitched their tents, and at his command they took them down (Numbers 9). It is enough for you, etc. Moses is commanded to depart from the mountain on which he had received the law, because a teacher ought not always to dwell on contemplation, but sometimes should come down to take care of himself and his neighbours; whence, Whether we are beside ourselves, it is to God; or whether we are sober, it is for you.
1.9: 1.9 And I said to you at that time, etc. Concerning this division of powers, in Exodus, before they came to Mount Sinai, it is written that Jethro, priest of Midian, Moses' kinsman, suggested this to him (Exodus 18). Hence it is rightly asked how these things agree with one another now, and at that time. But what Moses is here said to have said at that time: I am not able alone to bear you, etc., does not signify the time when they were setting out from Horeb, but the whole time in which, having set out from Egypt, they were lingering in the wilderness, and Moses persuaded his people of this not from his own counsel but from his kinsman's. At that time. The saints do all things at the opportune time; so God too, when the fullness of time came, sent his Son (Galatians 4).
1.11: 1.11 May the Lord God of your fathers add, etc. He teaches teachers to rejoice in the progress of those under them, to give thanks, and always to wish for better things. To this number, etc. Defined with God. He knows who are his, who numbers the multitude of the stars (2 Timothy 2). RABANUS. See how much is to be observed what Scripture says elsewhere: My son, meddle not with many matters (Ecclesiasticus 11). Consider also the words of Jethro giving counsel, for he says: Hear me, and I will give thee counsel, and God shall be with thee (Exodus 18). It seems to be signified that a mind too intent on human actions is in a way emptied of God, who is filled all the more, the more freely one is extended toward heavenly and eternal things.
1.13: 1.13 Give from among you. You give them, not I; as if to say, I do not wish to command you but to obey. I will appoint them. Note: to the subjects he grants the choice, but keeps the appointing for himself, lest the people despise or hate him, if it were not permitted to have the one they wanted. Tribunes. Chiliarchs, in Greek, that is, those who teach their subjects about the hope of the eternal reward. And centurions. Centurions, in Greek: those who hand on the heavenly commands to the perfect. Rightly are they put in charge who are endowed with the number one hundred, that is, with perfection: as it were they rule a hundred, while they lead to perfection. And commanders of fifty. In Greek: those who announce the works of penance. Deans, : those who, awaiting the denarius of the vineyard through the perfection of the number ten, prepare many to share in that same denarius.
1.17: 1.17 For it is the judgment of God; not of men, because in judging you are God's vicars, who accepts no person. But if it be hard. The greater ought to discern and judge all the greater and difficult matters, the lesser the small and easy ones.
1.19: 1.19 And when we had come to Kadesh-barnea, etc. That in the second year of its going out the people came into the desert of Paran, which is Kadesh; where, when the spies returned with the fruits of the land and reported what they had seen, they murmured against Moses and Aaron, and therefore, afflicted with the weariness of the long journey and with death, perished: this place will give clear evidence. Here it is to be noted that the forty-two encampments which they had from Egypt to the Jordan seem to fit only three courses of years: namely the first, the second, and the fortieth of the going out from Egypt. The first by a definite distinction contains twelve, the first at Rameses, entered on the fifteenth day of the first month, the last the wilderness of Sinai, added on the first day of the third month; and for eleven continuous months, for the sake of building the tabernacle and teaching the law, it was scarcely left. Of these twelve encampments only nine are expressed by name in Exodus; three are indistinctly signified under the name of the desert of Sin, which is said to lie between Elim and Sinai. The second year embraces twenty-one encampments. Of these, all being comprised without distinction in the order of the history under the name of the wilderness of Paran, only the first, the second, and the last, that is, the Graves of Lust, Hazeroth, and Kadesh, are distinguished by name. But in the catalogue of encampments all are shown equally, how many they are in number and by what name they are called. The first encampment, that is, the Graves of Lust, was entered in the second month of that same second year, on the twenty-second day of the month. For in the second year, as Scripture says, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they moved camp from the desert of Sinai, and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Paran, and they set out from the mountain of the Lord a journey of three days, until they came to the place of encampment, which, deservedly because of the people lusting after flesh, received the name of the Graves of Lust. On what day or month of that year they entered the last of these, that is, Kadesh, is not said; yet that it lies in the wilderness of Paran, and that it was reached in the same year, is not passed over in silence. For it is written: The people moved not from that place till Miriam was called back. And he set out from Hazeroth, pitching tents in the desert of Paran, where the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Send men to view the land of Canaan (Numbers 12, 13). Lest this be thought commanded and done at the encampment next after Hazeroth, rather than fulfilled in the last of those comprised under the name Paran, it is written below: And the spies of the land, returning after forty days, having gone round the whole region, came to Moses in Paran, which is Kadesh. In Deuteronomy also Moses says to the people: When you had come to Kadesh-barnea, I said to you: You are come to the mountain of the Amorite, etc., and you said: Send men to view the land, etc. (Deuteronomy 1). That they came to the same encampment in the second year of the going out, and yet from the sin of murmuring deserved to turn back, to wander long through the desert, and to fall here and there, Moses testifies in what follows, saying: You sat in Kadesh-barnea a long time, and setting out from there we came into the wilderness which leads to the Red Sea, as the Lord had said to me, and we went round Mount Seir a long time, and the time in which we walked from Kadesh-barnea to the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the whole generation of fighting men was consumed. Zered, however, is not the name of any of the forty-two encampments, but of a brook, to which, as is read in the book of Numbers, passing the eighteenth encampment named Iye-abarim, they came; leaving it, it says, they encamped over against Arnon, which is in the desert and projects into the borders of the Amorite, which, it is not hidden, was done in the fortieth year, which last year contains ten encampments of the very long way through the desert: the first of which, repeated with great labour, was the very same Kadesh of the desert of Sin, which they had left behind thirty-eight years before as their fault demanded, about which it is written: The children of Israel came into the desert of Sin in the first month, and the people abode in Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried in the same place. And when the people wanted water, they gathered together against Moses and Aaron, etc., until this: This is the water of contradiction, etc. (Numbers 20). It is to be noted that the same Kadesh was in the desert of Paran and in the desert of Sin, as Scripture relates, whence we conjecture that the part of the desert of Paran where Kadesh is is specially called Sin: but this Sin is not the Kadesh itself, which they passed through between Elim and Sinai soon after crossing the Red Sea, but another altogether, and written with other letters among the Hebrews. The second encampment of the same fortieth year is Mount Hor, on which Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month; the last, the plains of Moab above the Jordan against Jericho, where they stayed meditating on Deuteronomy until, Moses having died, with Joshua as leader, they crossed the Jordan on the first day of the tenth month. There are therefore twelve encampments of the first year, twenty-one of the second, and of the last year the twenty-first itself which is Kadesh, and nine others, so that all together they are forty-two.
23.1: 23.1 He shall not enter. All who live softly and do not accomplish manly work cannot remain in the congregation of the saints nor are worthy of entering the kingdom of heaven, which suffers violence, and the violent bear it away. Bastard. One degenerate in sense or morals; or one whom the perversity of heretics has made degenerate in the reception of the sacraments; or whom the rite of the Gentiles or of Judaism has stained. He will be received into the Church when with whole faith he has kept the decalogue of the law according to the institution of the Gospel, and, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, has renounced carnal conduct; whence: If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments (Matthew 19). And elsewhere: I am the door; by me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved (John 10).
23.3: 23.3 The Ammonite and the Moabite. AUGUSTINE, question 33. Another edition, etc., until they imputed to women, whom they preferred to preserve. Moabites. It signifies that heretics are always to be driven from the Church, as if to say, A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid.
23.4: 23.4 Because they would not meet you with, etc. The Hebrews relate that these nations, being kin to them, met those coming out of Egypt with bread only, though they knew we were suffering most from thirst in the desert, and therefore they were subjected to this curse. Mystically they designate heretics, who offer to those fleeing from the Egypt of this world toward the true land of promise polluted bread, not sweetened with the water of wisdom, and therefore they are alienated from the Church.
23.5: 23.5 And he turned. Because persecution is often the cause of greater prosperity. For to them that love God, all things work together unto good (Romans 8).
23.7: 23.7 Thou shalt not abhor the Edomite. The Edomite, bloody or earthly, signifies the flesh, whose matter is earthly: the Egyptian, that is, the dark one, the diseased body. We ought not to abhor our flesh, but to cherish it and give it what is necessary, yet not make care of it a matter of desires: He is, it says, thy brother, because we are of flesh and soul. Let us not abhor the Egyptian, that is, the body, in whose land we were strangers; for the soul, which has a heavenly origin, dwells in the body as a stranger, whence the Apostle: While we are in the body, we are absent from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5). They that are born of them, etc., that is, they will gradually become spiritual. By the Edomite and the Egyptian the present life is signified; although, renouncing it, we turn away from the Egyptian land, that is, from the former way of life and the concupiscence of the world, yet while we are subject to the necessities of this world we do not wholly extinguish the Egyptian nation: but, separated in a certain way, we are content with daily food and clothing; in the third generation they will enter the Church, because a worldly person can be joined to the saints of God when he has perfectly believed in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, or when he has been adorned with hope, faith, and charity.
23.9: 23.9 When. He instructs the spiritual soldiers of Christ, to whom it is said elsewhere: Every one that striveth for the mastery refraineth himself from all things (1 Corinthians 9). If. AUGUSTINE, On the Good of Marriage, chapter 20. The law sets down many things in sacraments and shadows of future things, etc., until not because a dead body is a sin, but it signifies the sin of a soul deserted by justice. Mystically GREGORY, Morals, book 9, chapter 40. If there be among you a man, who is defiled by a nocturnal pollution, etc. A nocturnal dream is a hidden temptation, etc., until and by the merits of the faithful it is to be presumed restored.
23.12: 23.12 Thou shalt have. God loves bodily cleanness: therefore he commanded that nothing foul remain in the camp. Mystically. GREGORY, Morals, book 31, chapter 32. Thou shalt have a place, etc. Weighed down by the burden of corruptible nature, certain superfluities of thoughts break out from the womb of our mind like the burden of the belly. But we ought to carry a peg under the girdle, that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have around us the sharp goad of compunction, which with the sorrow of penance may dig into the earth of our mind and hide what breaks out foul from us.
23.13: 23.13 In thy girdle. For the loins are girded with a girdle; therefore by the girdle the crushing of an evil will is designated, whence Job: He looseth the girdle of kings, and girdeth their loins with a cord (Job 2). Thou shalt cover with earth. Considering earthly frailty, we ought to cover our filth.
23.15: 23.15 Thou shalt not deliver the servant. AUGUSTINE, question 36. The Septuagint: Thou shalt not deliver the boy to his master who has been set beside thee by his master. Not that the master set him there, etc., until he explains this, saying: He will dwell among you in any place that shall please him (1 Kings 27).
23.17: 23.17 There shall be no harlot. AUGUSTINE, question 37. The Septuagint: There shall be no harlot, etc., until so what seemed right to us we treated there. Thou shalt not offer the hire of a harlot. AUGUSTINE, question 38. The Septuagint: Thou shalt not offer, etc., until it had to be said that it is an abomination to the Lord. The price of a dog, of a rapacious one. The Most High approveth not the gifts of the wicked. He that offereth sacrifice of the goods of the poor is as one that sacrificeth the son in the presence of his father (Ecclesiasticus 34).
23.19: 23.19 Thou shalt not lend to thy brother. He removes usury and avarice, and commands charity to be bestowed. And money which is forbidden to be given at usury, because it is a vice of cupidity to wish to exact what you know you did not lend. The Lord had this, and handed it over for distribution to the poor, and invited us to generosity of giving. There is another which we ought to give at usury; whence: Thou oughtest therefore to have committed my money to the bankers, and at my coming I should have received my own with usury (Matthew 25).
23.20: 23.20 But to the stranger. To the unbeliever or unjust man to whom we give money at usury, when for the word of preaching we demand faith, penance and good work.
23.21: 23.21 Thou shalt not delay to pay it. Whence Solomon: It is ruin to a man to make vows and afterwards to retract or delay (Proverbs 10).
23.24: 23.24 Going into thy neighbour's vineyard. In the church of another bishop, another may correct or confirm some people, but it is not permitted him to rule the whole people or to handle great affairs. Out. Outside the church it is not lawful to carry out this grace, because in one house the flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten.
23.25: 23.25 If thou go into. There are some places of Scripture which historically instil faith, some which morally instruct holy conduct; some show mysteries to be revered not according to the history but according to allegory. One must therefore enter cautiously into the standing grain of the neighbour, so that by discerning you pluck food, and not, by hurrying, incur the judgment on a reaped harvest.
24.1: 24.1 If he take. RABANUS on Deuteronomy, vol. 2. A man took a wife, etc., until as unworthy and polluted by error she remained abominable; whence: It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you, but because, etc. (Acts 13). AUGUSTINE, On the Sermon on the Mount, book 1. There were many causes in the law for putting away wives, etc., until that they who have wives be as though they had none (1 Corinthians 7). He shall write. Moses wrote this precept for the hardness of your heart, preferring to indulge divorce rather than have murder committed.
24.4: 24.4 To sin. He pollutes his land who stains his body with carnal desires. Therefore it is necessary that ambition for the present life be tamed quickly, lest it be able to rule. And once earthly action has been repelled, it is not to be taken up again: lest he look back who had put his hand to the plough.
24.5: 24.5 When he hath taken. As if to say, whoever binds himself to carnal desires and knows himself not suited for the government of the Church and for spiritual warfare: For no man, being a soldier to God, entangleth himself with secular business, that he may please him to whom he hath engaged himself (2 Timothy 2); whence: Impose hands lightly on no man. ISIDORE. He takes away the upper millstone who says to one weeping over a sin: You will not have pardon for what you have committed. He takes away the lower who, flattering sin, says: Do as much evil as you like, God is merciful and ready to pardon; both millstones are usefully held if there is hope with fear that amends, and fear with hope. GREGORY, Morals, book 33, chapter 16. Thou shalt not take the lower millstone to pledge, etc. To take we sometimes say for to offer, etc., until and he fears in vain who does not trust.
24.7: 24.7 Thou shalt take away. AUGUSTINE, question 39. Scripture says this constantly, etc., until which, expounding, he says: Let him that stole, steal no more (Ephesians 4).
24.8: 24.8 The plague of leprosy. Note that this infirmity befalls men on account of sin, as with Uzziah, who usurped the priesthood.
24.10: 24.10 When thou shalt demand again. AUGUSTINE, question 41. It belongs to the work of mercy that the one taking a pledge not enter the house, etc., until having nowhere to sleep. Is it not so? He who preaches the Gospel, let him live by the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9). For the workman is worthy of his hire (Luke 10).
24.16: 24.16 They shall not be put to death. AUGUSTINE, question 42. The law also says, etc., until he did not wish three or four to be understood.
24.17: 24.17 Thou shalt not pervert. AUGUSTINE, question 43. The Septuagint: Thou shalt not turn aside the judgment of the stranger and orphan and widow. Thou shalt not take the widow's garment in pledge. Why does he not say, etc., until continence in them is praised, desolation is not commended. Widow. The widow is the soul formerly joined to the devil, whose garment of faith, once converted, is not to be taken away.
24.19: 24.19 Thou shalt not return. Through envy of the Gentiles, who are strangers to the testaments of God.
24.20: 24.20 If you gather the fruits. Even if the proud and wicked gather, he does mercy who leaves behind with this intention, that the needy may have. Moreover, when these things are commanded to the people, those who are not in need are warned not to seek them. But if they do seek them, they are to be judged as plunderers of the poor. Thy vineyard. The vineyard from which wine is gathered, which maketh glad the heart of man (Psalm 103).
25.1: 25.1 If there be a cause. AUGUSTINE, question 45. The Septuagint: But if there be a quarrel between men, etc., until so also sins which seem to be committed not against God but against man: some are worthy of death, some of the scourge.
25.3: 25.3 Forty. Forty is completed by ten taken four times. We consist according to the body of four elements: the precepts of the decalogue are taken by ten. He commands, therefore, that judgment or vengeance, in which the sin of the flesh is punished, be ordered according to the precepts, and he wishes all the precepts in the decalogue to be understood. ISIDORE. In the number forty this present time is figured, etc., until there we shall be found without sin.
25.4: 25.4 The mouth of the ox that treadeth out. ISIDORE. In the ox the life of those who work is expressed, of whom it is said: The workman is worthy of his hire (Luke 10). Scripture therefore wishes carnal things to be supplied to those from whom we receive spiritual things, who, occupied in teaching, cannot provide for themselves what is necessary.
25.5: 25.5 When. AUGUSTINE, question 46. The Septuagint: If brothers dwelt together before, etc., until or adoption made another father whom Joseph could have. He shall be dead. He suffered and ascended into heaven, the synagogue still remaining barren. But he shall take, etc. Him who is able to rule, in whose face the woman spits against his will. For he who does not care to benefit others with spiritual gifts, the Church, reproaching even his goods, as it were throws spittle in his face.
25.9: 25.9 The shoe. Of which it is said: Your feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace (Ezekiel 6). If we care for our neighbour as for ourselves, we protect each foot with a shoe; but he who, thinking of his own advantage, neglects his neighbours loses, as it were, the shoe of one foot, with disgrace. From the foot, that is, he will show him deprived of the reward of preaching. For the feet of teachers are shod, because, fortified by the examples of the fathers who went before, they have imitated the steps of their preaching. He is shod on both feet who benefits himself and others.
25.11: 25.11 And one against another. The Catholic and the heretic, whose contention is perpetual because their intention is unlike: for one defends falsehood, the other truth, and error must be resisted, lest the fool seem wise to himself. And she shall pity. Through false disgrace or abominable action he will have wished to stain the conduct of the Catholic or defame his teaching. The secrets. The weaker members of the Church, which they will wish to deceive by flattering or deride by insulting.
25.13: 25.13 Thou shalt not have in thy bag. In Leviticus the same is forbidden. Solomon also says: Diverse weights and diverse measures, both are abominable before God (Proverbs 20). ISIDORE. Thou shalt not have in thy bag. Spiritually also we must take care not to have different weights in our heart, that is, softening for ourselves the rule of strictness, and overwhelming those to whom we preach the word of God with stricter precepts as if with heavier weights. When we do this, we weigh out the reward and fruit of the Lord's precepts by a different weight, whence: Diverse weights are an abomination to the Lord (Proverbs 20).
25.17: 25.17 Remember what. The Hebrews relate that Amalek killed the lepers and those with issues of seed, and others placed outside the camp, and they say these were the rear of the Lord's host. Amalek licking blood. These are the demons who oppose us who go out through baptism from the spiritual Egypt, and who, by suggesting sins, strive to kill those last in virtues and wearied on the road of this life. When the Lord has given the opportunity, we ought altogether to overthrow them and in every way cast out and destroy their suggestions, lest, if we keep any remnants as Saul did, we be overthrown with them as disobedient.
26.1: 26.1 And when thou art come, etc. As the Israelites in the promised land are commanded to offer their firstfruits in thanksgiving because they were rescued from Egypt, so we, entering through the spiritual Jordan, that is, baptism, into the land of the Church, should place in the basket of our way of life the firstfruits of good work, and offer them to God on the altar of the Catholic faith, that our priest Christ may receive them, and there confess to the Lord, saying that the Syrian, which is interpreted lofty or moistening, that is, the devil, pursued our father, that is, the first-formed man, to deprive him, deceived through pride, gluttony and avarice, of the possession of paradise, whence as an exile he sojourned in the Egypt of this world with a small number, because many followed idolatry and few believers remained. But after the law was given, more rose up, receiving the knowledge and faith of the one God, and the Egyptians, that is, the demons, afflicted them, laying upon them the heaviest burdens of sins. But God looked upon the affliction and labour of the human race, and sent his Son, who is called his hand and arm, to rescue them from the power of darkness and translate them into the kingdom of light. So he gave us the land flowing with milk and honey, that is, the powerful Church, where there is the milk of innocence and the honeycomb of doctrine, by which little ones are nourished, and the honey of sweet and manifold wisdom, by which the perfect are satisfied.
26.10: 26.10 Which the Lord God hath given, etc. As if to say: I offer only what he gave; for every good is from God. Of the Lord thy God. Who will keep it as if under his eyes, and will repay in that day as just judge.
26.11: 26.11 Thou shalt feast, at the spiritual banquet, of which it is said: Eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved (Canticles 5). And the Levite, the true minister of God, taken from among men, and appointed for men in the things that appertain to God.
26.12: 26.12 When thou hast completed: that Tobias fulfilled this of the law, but those who were far from the temple in the third year gave the collected tithes of three years to the poor and the Levites who dwelt with them.
27.2: 27.2 Stones. Teachers ought to lay aside all roughness, and therefore to appear splendid, having the law written in their hearts.
27.4: 27.4 When therefore. ISIDORE. How this was done, etc., until who are worthy of the building of the altar. Those who proceed beside Mount Gerizim, chosen to bless, figure those who come to salvation not from fear of punishment but kindled by love of the heavenly promise. Those who proceed beside Mount Ebal, on which the curses were pronounced, are those who do the precepts of the law not from love of blessings or promises but from fear of punishments. All, however, proceed around the ark, because they do not depart from the bosom of the Church. But nobler are those who serve from charity than those who serve from fear of punishment. Jesus alone can know minds of this kind, and station some on Mount Gerizim to bless, others on Mount Ebal to curse, not that they should receive the curse, but that they may beware of the curses written and appointed for sinners, and repent from fear of punishment.
27.13: 27.13 And they shall pronounce. Because the priest ought to preach the word to the people urgently and powerfully, that they may know, if they transgress the commandments of God, what dangers await; if they obey, what benefits follow, namely consolation in the present life and eternal reward in the future. The curses and blessings pertain historically to those who love earthly happiness or dread unhappiness. But Christians especially must take care lest through disobedience they suffer spiritual poverty; for perfect men often lack earthly things, while the abundance of virtues is always present, whence: Even unto this hour we both hunger and thirst, and are naked, etc. (1 Corinthians 4). Cursed. Not only the idolatry of images is forbidden, but every error of heretics. For they are artificers of vanity and of superstitious doctrine, who from their own heart fashion for themselves what gods they will.
27.16: 27.16 All the people. All ought to praise good things and detest evil ones, prelates and subjects alike.
27.17: 27.17 Cursed be he that removeth the landmarks. This is he who, not content with Catholic faith and doctrine, introduces superstitions and sects.
27.20: 27.20 Cursed be he that sleepeth with. Every incest is an abomination, but it especially strikes heretics and schismatics, who corrupt by error the bride of Christ, who is the father and creator of all. Tropologically, however, it forbids anyone, by imitating the wicked action of his father, to defame him and reveal his shame.
27.21: 27.21 Cursed. Cursed is he who follows the folly of the Gentiles. A man or woman who clings to such mixing, not through frailty but perseveringly, is guilty of death.
27.22: 27.22 He sleeps, that is, he stains the soul of another by teaching wrongly or by showing wicked examples. For our Father is one, God, and our mother the Church, and we are all brothers or sisters.
27.23: 27.23 With his mother-in-law. The mother-in-law is the concupiscence of wicked action, because the concupiscence of every sin is a mother. Let us therefore attend diligently to resist concupiscence, lest we fulfil what we desire.
27.24: 27.24 Cursed. In whatever way, to kill a man is sin. It seems strange, then, why he pronounced a curse only on him who strikes secretly. But perhaps to strike secretly is to hate in the heart, whence: He that hateth his brother is a murderer (John 3). And elsewhere: Hate not thy brother in thy heart (Leviticus 19).
27.26: 27.26 Cursed be he that abideth not. This sentence comprehends generally the commandments of the law, past and present and to be spoken, and is the graver the more general it is. For who can abide in all the words of the law without transgression, since Paul also says: As many as are of the works of the law are under a curse? (Galatians 3). No one could escape this curse, not even the lawgiver, except Christ, whence: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us, etc.
28.1: 28.1 But if thou wilt hear. As he foretells curses and punishments to the disobedient, so he promises blessings and rewards to the obedient.
28.4: 28.4 The fruit of thy womb. He marks the various orders of subjects. For some furnish bodily aids to teachers; others can labour at what has been commanded them; others, content in simplicity, strive by innocence of life to please God: each one has his own gift from God.
28.5: 28.5 Blessed be thy barns. The reward of good intention, even if the will does not have its effect, because there is peace to men of good will, etc. (Luke 2).
28.6: 28.6 Coming in. He comes in by the door who inwardly meditates and handles the Catholic faith according to the will of God: he goes out when he makes the same manifest before men to the praise of God.
28.7: 28.7 Before thy face. That you may rejoice: The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge (Psalm 57).
28.8: 28.8 And he will bless. Giving increase and happy success to good works. Heaven. The prophets and apostles, of whom it is said, The heavens shew forth the glory of God: whom the Lord opens, when through them he bestows abundance of doctrine, so that the hearts of the carnal, watered by this shower, may put forth the shoots of good works. Thou shalt lend. That is, there will be so much abundance for you that you will be able to give money to the nations, but they not so much to you. Or, ecclesiastical doctrine is understood. Thou shalt lend to nations. The Church lends to many nations when she dispenses divine gifts to the peoples. Nor does she take interest, because she seeks not present but future recompense. For she excels all, and is the head of the world, not the tail. She is always above, and not beneath; because although she suffers the oppressions and persecutions of the wicked in the world, yet she is stronger than her adversaries and surpasses all in faith and virtue. Hence, The Lord will make thee the head, etc.
28.14: 28.14 Thou shalt not decline. AUGUSTINE, question 48. The Septuagint: Thou shalt not pass over any of the words, etc., until nor are they to be worshipped on account of these.
28.15: 28.15 But if thou wilt not hear. As he promised a blessing to those who keep the commandments, so he pronounces a curse on the negligent.
28.22: 28.22 May the Lord strike thee. AUGUSTINE, Enchiridion, chapter 98. Who would be so impious in folly as to say that God cannot turn the evil wills of men, whichever he wishes, when he wishes, where he wishes, to good? But when he does it, he does it by mercy; when he does not, he does not by judgment, he who has mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardeneth. And with corrupted air. A life polluted by carnal uncleanness. Carnal life is expressed by air, because the human body is given life by the breath of air.
28.23: 28.23 Let the heaven be. He compares the elements by which fruits are nourished to the hardest metals, because the sins of men change the order of things, and things established for the comfort of the human race, whence: The whole world shall fight for him against the unwise. The heaven is brazen for the transgressors of the law, when they deserve no clemency from the holy teachers but the hardest discipline, since they themselves have not a heart of flesh and a soft mind, but a heart of stone and iron. As the law was given to a hard people on stone, so that the receiver might be figured by the gift.
28.24: 28.24 May the Lord give dust as rain upon thy land: as if to say, as dust and ashes bear no fruit, so may the doctrine poured into you not rouse the shoots of virtues, but foretell eternal destruction. For dust designates the barrenness of good works, ashes burning; because the chaff of sinners will be burned with unquenchable fire.
28.25: 28.25 And mayest thou be scattered. As the captive Jews were dispersed through the breadth of the world because they were gathered against God, so the generation of the wicked, scattered by unclean spirits, is troubled by kinds of punishments, whence: Thy enemies shall perish; and all they shall be scattered that work iniquity (Psalm 91).
28.27: 28.27 May the Lord strike thee with the ulcer of Egypt. Ulcers: painful and festering malice. Blisters: swollen pride. Scab and itch: burning anger and the madness of fury. These are inflicted in the present as a fitting punishment for sins: after this life, what is signified in the hinder parts, they will bear the stench of their crimes in eternal torments. May the Lord strike thee. Heretics and schismatics, while the Gospel shines throughout the world, wrapped in the blindness of error, exercising their madness, contradict the Catholic faith. Therefore they bear the slander of the Church and are crushed by the truth. They were mad and blind when, seeing the miracles of Christ, they said they were done in Beelzebub, and denied that Christ is God (Matthew 7), and did not see the truth, that is, understand it.
28.29: 28.29 And mayest thou grope. There was darkness when Jesus was crucified until the ninth hour, as there was darkness in the hearts of the Jews. Thou shalt not make straight: neither did they believe when Christ preached, nor were they willing to be set straight by penance.
28.30: 28.30 Thou shalt take a wife, and another, etc. By the wife is understood the people joined to heretics, with whom the devil fornicates while it is seduced into error. The animals are seized by heretics when the subjects are freed from them: when they themselves are deprived of life and doctrine. The Church also converts to her own use the substance which the Jews had prepared for themselves singularly by teaching and writing.
28.33: 28.33 The fruits of thy land. The whole usefulness of the ceremonies has been transferred to the Church. She enjoys this abundance, the Jews perish in want, whence it is said through Isaiah: My servants shall eat, and you shall be hungry (Isaiah 65).
28.35: 28.35 In the knees and in the legs. Let him take away strength and steadiness. Or, let him be struck in the knees whose last works are condemned. From the sole of the foot. As from the beginning of an evil will to the perfection of the work you have practised malice, whence from the sole of the foot unto the top of the head there is no soundness therein (Isaiah 1). This was fulfilled in the last captivity.
28.36: 28.36 And the Lord shall bring thee. Heretics or bad Catholics, who despise the precepts of God, are made captive by demons and various vices. As the servant, so the master, and the king as the people, the teacher as the disciple. And the king. Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians led Hosea king of Samaria into captivity with the ten tribes: Nebuchadnezzar took captive Jehoiachin, and Zedekiah king of Judah with the people.
28.38: 28.38 Seed, etc. We too must take care not to lose the bread that strengtheneth man's heart, and the wine that maketh glad, and the oil that maketh the face to shine.
28.43: 28.43 The stranger. The rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles is openly signified, whence: The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and shall be given to a nation yielding the fruits thereof, and elsewhere: So shall the last be first, and the first last. RABANUS on Deuteronomy, vol. 2. The stranger that is conversant with thee, etc. The Creator of all, through the mystery of his incarnation, etc., until and shall have counted the blood of the testament unclean.
28.66: 28.66 And thy life shall be. Nothing is worse among the curses that befell the Jews through the deserving of pride than to see their life, that is, the Son of God, hanging, and not to believe in him. But when curses are spoken from prophecy, they are not from an evil wish but are foretold. It could also be rendered thus to the Jews: You shall see your life hanging, and you shall not believe your life, that is, amid the threats and deceits of enemies you will see your life hanging in uncertainty.
29.1: 29.1 These are the words, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 49 on Deuteronomy. The Septuagint: These are the words of the covenant, etc., until to Abraham concerning circumcision or to Noah.
29.3: 29.3 Great temptations, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 50. And the Lord God hath not given you a heart to know, etc., until since the judgments of God, though hidden, are just.
29.6: 29.6 You have not eaten bread, etc. AUGUSTINE. From this it appears that the Israelites, etc., until not the beginning of war, but the beginning of wine.
29.18: 29.18 Lest perhaps there be. AUGUSTINE, question 52. The Septuagint: Is there any among you, etc., until he had not coveted another's wife for himself.
29.19: 29.19 The drunken with the thirsty, and the Lord, etc. That is, lest anyone full of malice and idolatry seduce him who thirsts to learn and know the truth, as heretics do.
30.11: 30.11 This commandment, which I, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 54. The Septuagint: Because this commandment, etc., until without which, if they are done outwardly with the hands and are not done in the heart, the precepts of God are not fulfilled.
30.14: 30.14 The word is nigh unto thee, etc. That is, the commandments of God are moderated and tempered to human strength. This can be taken of the incarnation of Christ, who, having assumed humanity, was seen upon earth and conversed among men.
31.7: 31.7 And he called. The words of Moses to Joshua signify that Christ distributes the land of the living to each according to his merits, and fulfils all the promises of God. For he himself brings the people into the promised land. Under him as leader we enter the heavenly homeland, he who says: No man cometh to the Father, but by me (John 14). And: No man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven (John 3); for he is united and ascends through him.
31.10: 31.10 After seven years. In which the present life is signified, which turns in the number seven; or the time of the old law on account of the sabbath. After seven years, then, in the year of remission, the law is commanded to be read in the assembly: because when the observance of the law is completed, the spiritual law succeeds. Whence: When the fullness of the time was come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, etc. (Ephesians 4).
31.24: 31.24 Therefore after Moses had written. Deuteronomy is entrusted to the Levites, because the Gospel of Christ is laid up in memory by the ministry of true priests in the Church, which is the ark of the Lord, where heavenly treasures are stored. There are the two tables of the testament, namely the books of the law and the Gospel. There is the urn containing manna, that is, the flesh of Christ, in which is the food of eternal life; there is the rod of Aaron, which had budded, because there is the priesthood of Christ, which abides for ever, or, in perpetuity, that it may be there against thee for a testimony. The words of the law are for salvation to those who keep them, for those who despise them a testimony of contumacy and disobedience: whence: There is one that accuseth you, Moses, in whom you trust. For if you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also: for he wrote of me (John 5); and elsewhere: The word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him (John 12).
31.30: 31.30 Moses therefore spoke. The words of Moses are not to be taken simply, because according to the history he reproaches the perfidy of the Israelites ungrateful to God the giver, and allegorically he instructs the holy Church, and by tropology urges to honesty of conduct. In history, therefore, truth is to be kept, in allegory mysteries, in tropology the usefulness of discipline, that so we may be carried forward to heavenly contemplation. It is also to be noted what is said: Moses spoke the words of this canticle, etc., so that he who praises God with the mouth may not contradict by deed. Praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner (Ecclesiasticus 13).
32.1: 32.1 Hear, O ye heavens. At the beginning he calls the greatest elements to witness, so that if they neglect the commandments, he may punish them, convicted by the testimony of these. In Hebrew shamayim, that is, heavens, which is plural and masculine in gender, but he wished it understood in the singular, as we say singular cities, Thebes and Athens. Hear, O ye heavens. RABANUS. Let the heavens hear the allegory, the earth the history. Hear, O ye heavens, etc. Some think heaven and earth are summoned to hear as if animate, according to that: Who looketh upon the earth and maketh it tremble (Psalm 103), though this belongs to the power of God, not to their understanding.
32.2: 32.2 Let it grow. He compares the doctrine of the law to rain and dew, because it demands from the hearts of the faithful the shoots of spiritual fruit. For these are the field and vineyard of God. Like that of Isaiah: As the rain and the snow come down from heaven, and return no more thither, but soak the earth, and water it, and make it spring (Isaiah 55).
32.3: 32.3 The name. He shows what the rain is. For to call upon the name of the Lord is to preach the Gospel: he who hears and does it will possess the fruit of life. Of God. Whence: So the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the furniture of them: and on the seventh day God ended his work (Genesis 2), which is the redemption of the human race, which he showed us when, completing the spiritual sabbath, he rested in the sepulchre.
32.5: 32.5 They have sinned against him, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 55. The Septuagint: Blameworthy sons have not sinned against him. For he who sins, etc., until in that they did not hurt him by their sin, but themselves. And not. Because not of faith. For he gave them power to be made the sons of God, to them that believe in his name. Of unbelievers, however, it is said: You are of your father the devil. A perverse generation. Of which in the Gospel: An evil and adulterous generation seeketh a sign (Matthew 12). And elsewhere: Ye brood of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come? (Luke 3).
32.6: 32.6 Is not he, etc. The one God, creator and maker of all, from whom and through whom and in whom are all things. A reversed order. For first God created by arranging that it should be, second he made by forming, third he possessed by ruling. He created: he created when he established the matter from which it could be formed. Foolish therefore and unwise, because he does not worship his Creator and maker with due reverence: forgetful of that benefit by which God rescued him from the hand of enemies and possessed him, led him through the Red Sea, gave manna from heaven, he himself ungrateful worshipped idols, saying: These are thy gods, O Israel, that have brought thee out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 32).
32.7: 32.7 Thy father. The teacher of the law and preacher of the Gospel, by whose teaching and example you may be instructed.
32.8: 32.8 When the Most High divided, etc. As if to say, although the multitude of men is innumerable, the Lord chose only the children of Israel as his inheritance, to whom he made known his power and his secrets by the signs of the law and the prophets. He set. GREGORY, Homily 4 on the Gospels. Another edition, etc., until and they ascend into their lot by likeness of conduct.
32.9: 32.9 But the Lord's portion is his people. When God created all the nations, he chose only the Israelites, whom he glorified with knowledge of himself, with signs and miracles.
32.10: 32.10 He found him. Because on Sinai he entered into a covenant with him, gave manna, brought water from the rock, supplied quails; and in the wilderness for forty years, leading them round about, he taught them his commandments. He led him about. By spreading the Church through the globe, directing her into the way of his commandments. He kept. Many were laid low in the desert, but after they transgressed the commandments of God.
32.11: 32.11 As the eagle. The eagle, according to the naturalists, is named from the sharpness of its eyes, and sees so acutely that when it is borne over the seas on motionless wing and is not visible to human sight, it sees little fishes swimming in the sea, and, descending like a missile, draws the seized prey by its wings to the shore. It also beats its fledglings with its wings and urges them to fly. So Christ, exhorting us by words and examples, carries us to high places, that we may follow where he has gone before; whence: Wheresoever the body shall be, there shall the eagles also be gathered together (Matthew 24). Exalted also above the heavens and withdrawn from human sight, he sees with eyes of mercy those swimming in the sea of this world, and by the wings of love draws them to the shore of eternal security. Whence: And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself (John 12). As the eagle, etc. The eagle, they say, when it sees its young fledging, turns them to the sun, and nurtures the one that gazes at the rays of the sun with unflinching sight, and if one turns away its eyes, it neglects it as degenerate; it urges the young to fly and supports the weary with its wings: so God invites us to the true Sun, has compassion on our infirmities, and supports us with the wings of grace. Provoking. The Lord provoked his people to possess the land of Canaan, helped them, and protected them from enemies.
32.12: 32.12 The Lord. The Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God. He does not say the Father alone, lest he exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit, but the Lord alone, that is, God. The Lord. Heretics have as many lords as they worship errors.
32.13: 32.13 High. Palestine, which is mountainous; Egypt is flat and low. The Church, which is lofty in virtue and knowledge. In which the fruit of the fields is eaten, because there the good seed, that is, the word of God, sprouts. There is the thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold fruit, so that each may eat sufficiently according to his capacity. And that he might suck. GREGORY, Homily 26 on the Gospels. That he might suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the hardest stone. This is nowhere read to have happened according to the history, etc., until the gift of the devil through the anointing of the Holy Spirit. Honey, literally, signifies abundance of all things.
32.14: 32.14 Of the sons. Bashan is a region abounding in cattle because of its pastures: whence it was given to the Reubenites and Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, because they had many cattle. And goats. Which signify penitents, because they were offered for sin. It is not enough for the faithful to receive gifts of virtues unless they take care to repent of what they have committed. Whence: Wash me yet more from my iniquity (Psalm 50). He calls goats those who by their example minister works of penance to others, although they have not committed grave sins: for they weep over sins of thought as if they were deeds. With the marrow of wheat. Of the body of Christ; whence: Unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground, etc. (John 12).
32.15: 32.15 The beloved grew fat, etc. As the Jews, fattened with benefits, became idolaters, so some Christians turn the received mystery of the body and blood of the Lord into their own perdition.
32.16: 32.16 They provoked. Some become heretics, others idolaters, who fashion idols and abominations for themselves from the heart.
32.17: 32.17 New and late. Departing from the worship of God, they found for themselves gods whom their fathers worshipped.
32.20: 32.20 And he said: I will hide, etc. Nothing is graver than to be deprived of the vision of God; whence: Cast me not away from thy face (Psalm 50). Likewise: Turn not away thy face, etc. (Psalm 88). They have provoked me, etc. As if to say: as they have angered me by worshipping a multitude of false gods and rejecting me, so I will anger them by taking up a multitude of nations and rejecting them. And I will provoke, etc. By handing them over to the Gentiles, who were once not a people, but now are the people of God. Likewise Christians who, abandoning the truth, decline into errors are handed over to malignant spirits, who have lost angelic dignity. They are rightly called a foolish nation, hating justice, loving iniquity.
32.22: 32.22 A fire is kindled, etc. GREGORY, Morals, book 18, chapter 12. Of those whom scourges condemn and do not free, it is written: Thou hast struck them, and they have not grieved, etc. For these the scourges begin in this life and will abide for ever; whence Moses: A fire is kindled in my wrath, and shall burn even to the lowest hell. Of the present striking it is said: A fire is kindled in my wrath (Jeremiah 15); of the eternal follows: And shall burn even to the lowest hell (Psalm 88). Yet God does not judge twice for the same thing: for it is one scourge that begins temporally and is consummated in eternal punishments. And shall devour the earth. Others: They shall eat the earth and its offspring, that is, the flesh, for the works of lust, an eternal flame will burn; for the offspring of the flesh are the works of carnal concupiscence, which are fornication, uncleanness and the like.
32.24: 32.24 Birds with biting, who eat the seed by the wayside. The teeth of beasts, etc. Beasts and serpents with furious teeth drag the reprobate over the earth, when what they first persuaded carnal people by flattery in order to seduce them, they furiously demand from the sinners in order to torment them.
32.25: 32.25 Without. The burning of eternal fire will torment the body, and the greatness of distress the mind; whence: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched (Isaiah 56). The young man. That is, no age will be spared, because idolatry has stained all.
32.26: 32.26 I will make to cease from among men. They were cast out of their land and dispersed through the whole world. Generally, sinners will be taken from the land of the saints, and their memory; whence: Therefore will God destroy thee for ever, he will pluck thee out, and remove thee from thy dwelling place, and thy root out of the land of the living, etc. (Psalm 51).
32.27: 32.27 I have deferred. Lest they blaspheme my name, yet I have not taken away vengeance.
32.30: 32.30 How. He shows such fear of the Jewish nation, after they sinned against the Lord, that one of the enemies would chase a thousand of them, and two ten thousand, that is, few the many.
32.31: 32.31 Judges. Approvers; even those who worship idols understand that there is one God who made heaven and earth.
32.32: 32.32 Of the vineyard, etc. It signifies the wickedness of heretics, who received pure spiritual doctrine from the holy teachers, but corrupted it by their own poison and perverted it into the bitterness of gall and wormwood. Jerusalem is often compared to Sodom and Gomorrah; whence: Hear the word of the Lord, ye princes of Sodom, give ear to the law of our God, ye people of Gomorrah (Isaiah 1). Most bitter clusters. The fruits, namely, are most bitter works, for they offered wine mixed with gall.
32.33: 32.33 The gall of dragons. As if they retain within themselves the poison of malice, lest they receive the medicine of salvation and correction. Heretics, like serpents, hide bitterness and poison to harm the unwary.
32.35: 32.35 Revenge is mine, etc. Paul took from this place: Vengeance is mine; I will repay (Romans 12), according to merits. In due time. As if to say, when I shall take a time, I will judge justices (Psalm 74). Hence to Moses praying for the people he said: In the day of revenge I will visit this sin also of theirs (Exodus 32). The day of destruction is at hand. To each. For whatever has an end is very brief, if compared to eternity. According to the history of the Jews vengeance hastens, because in a short time they lost place and nation and all prosperity, since they killed the prophets and the Saviour.
32.36: 32.36 The Lord will judge. By discerning from the wicked, according to that: Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause (Psalm 42). He shall see that their hand is weakened. Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly, for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, shall be in hell (Ecclesiastes 9).
32.37: 32.37 Where are their gods? As if to say: the idols in which they trusted, or riches or honours or the pleasures of the world, profit nothing, for they carry nothing with them from all their labour.
32.39: 32.39 See ye that I alone am, etc. A general admonition: as if, leaving idolatry or heresy and spurning all uncleannesses, turn to the true God. I will kill. GREGORY, Morals, book 7, chapter 18. He kills that he may make alive, he strikes that he may heal, etc., until and makes them sensitive by the ardour of charity.
32.40: 32.40 I will lift up. Another edition: I will lift up my hand to heaven, and will swear by my right hand, and I will say: I live for ever. To lift up or raise the hand of God to heaven is to show the power of his eternity excelling over all things. To swear by the right hand, that is, by the Son, who is the right hand of the Father, is to confirm his promises in the sight of men and to reveal his eternity to those who believe in him through the Gospel, because his power is an everlasting power (Daniel 7).
32.42: 32.42 Arrows. The demons, of whom Job says: The arrows of the Lord are in me (Job 6); as if to say: I will exercise so great a vengeance as could suffice even for demons. And of the captivity. The heads of captives were shaved; those who were sold were said to be sold under the crown. Of the captivity. The head of enemies is laid bare when the counsel of the wicked mind, by which it supposed it could sin with impunity, is proved vain. The heads of enemies are also the masters, on whom the final vengeance will overflow; whence: Blood came out of the press, even to the horses' bridles (Apocalypse 14), that is, the vengeance of torments even to the rulers of the peoples.
32.43: 32.43 For the blood. In the judgment the people of God will be praised, when it appears glorious, and the enemies will be punished by just retribution.
32.49: 32.49 Go up into the mountain. Abarim is interpreted passage; Nebo, in conclusion. Nebo is said to be a mountain in the land of Moab opposite Jericho, above the Jordan, on the brow of Pisgah, near Mount Peor, from which the region around it is still called Pisgah. Moses therefore dies in Abarim and on Mount Nebo opposite Jericho beyond the Jordan: because the law and circumcision went forward up to Christ and the sacrament of baptism, and there was concluded, because Christ is the end of the law. Moses saw the promised land but did not enter it, because in the spirit he foresaw, and in the law foretold, the coming grace of Christ, but did not see him present. Whence: Many just men and prophets have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them (Matthew 13).
33.1: 33.1 This is the blessing. Well did he place the blessing at the end of Deuteronomy, because Christ, after the completion of the Gospel, about to ascend into heaven, blessed his disciples with raised hands. The blessing with which he blessed the children of Israel in Deuteronomy, which is the second law, pertains to the grace of the New Testament, in which the mysteries of the ancient law are unlocked, and the true Israelites obtain the blessing, foretold through Moses the man of God, through the man Christ. Well is the blessing given as the death of Moses draws near, because, the shadow of the law dying, the truth of heavenly gifts is opened. Foreseeing, then, the coming of the Saviour and the grace of the New Testament, and setting it forth as if past, Moses, in the voice of the primitive Church, exults rejoicing, saying: The Lord came from Sinai, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 36. Another text, etc., until whence: Rejoice, ye nations, with his people. Because blindness in part has happened in Israel, until the fullness, etc. (Romans 11). Moses the man. Moses signifies the law, which before death, that is, before it was ended in him, foretold that the Church was to be blessed in Christ.
33.2: 33.2 The Lord came from Sinai. Sinai is interpreted my amphora, or my measure, or commandment. Seir, hairy or rough. Paran, their ferocity, or fruitful. Sinai therefore figures the Old Testament, because, holding a fixed measure of commandments according to the decree of the decalogue, it knew how to forbid, not to help: nor does it free by the spirit of love, but binds its subjects by fear of punishment. Whence: One indeed from Mount Sinai, engendering unto bondage, etc. (Galatians 4). The Lord therefore came from Sinai, that is, from the law and the prophets he became known to believers. For he comes from there when he becomes known there to one who reads and understands. Whence: Beginning at Moses and all the prophets (Luke 24), he expounded to the disciples, to whose hearts he desired to come. From Seir he rose according to the flesh, namely from the Jews, most rough with the thicket of malice and perfidy, and by the rising of a new light, like the true sun of justice, he enlightened the faithful. Whence: Unto us shall the sun of justice arise (Malachi 4). And elsewhere: A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall spring up from Israel (Numbers 24). The Lord, etc. Sinai is interpreted temptation. The Lord therefore came from Sinai, because he took our flesh, in which he was to be tempted. And from Seir, etc. Which is also Edom or Esau. This is the people of the Jews, who by desire of gluttony, as for a dish of lentils, lost the glory of the birthright, and, supplanted by the faith of the younger people, lost the grace of the blessing. From Seir he rose for us, etc. They went round this mountain for a long time, and received some precepts on it. Seir, that is, rough or hairy, signifies the Gentile world, which was dreadful with sins; from it the Lord arose, who at the end from the Church of the Gentiles will preach to the Jews, because a remnant shall be saved. He appeared from Mount Paran, etc. Which is interpreted fruitful, because from the Church of the Gentiles the faith of Christ, fruitful in virtues, was preached to the Jews. Christ therefore appeared from Paran; because the more the ferocity of unbelievers blazed against him, the higher grew the knowledge of his divinity. For the more he was hidden amid the insults of the passion, the more he shone forth by the power of the resurrection; and those who first persecuted him with the ferocity of unbelief afterwards clung to him with the ardour of love; of whom is added: And with him thousands of saints. In his right hand a fiery law. The tables, namely, on which is the law, which purges and burns sins. The right hand of the Father is also the Son, who brought the law of charity, saying: I am come to cast fire on the earth, etc. (Luke 12). In his right hand a fiery law. The right hand, the Gospel, through which eternal blessedness is promised; which is called the right hand, not temporal as in the law, which is called the left. Whence: His right hand shall embrace me. In this right hand is the fiery law, that is, charity kindled by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect. Whence he says: Love is the fulness of the law (Romans 13). And elsewhere: A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another (John 13). This, poured into the apostles by the fiery tongues of the Holy Spirit, wrote the whole fullness of the law as with the finger of God, and made them fervent in spirit and shining in work. But because it was given not to one people, like the law of Moses, but to all, he adds: He loved the peoples.
33.3: 33.3 He loved. Whence: Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life, etc. (John 15). All. Without respect of persons; whence: He that feareth God, and worketh justice, is acceptable to him (Acts 10). All the saints. Sanctified, namely, in the name of him who heard: Be ye holy, for I am holy, etc. (Leviticus 19). In his hand. That is, in the power by which they are protected. Whence: No man shall pluck them out of my hand, etc. (John 10). These through charity are one kingdom in the hand of the Lord; whence Isaiah: And thou shalt be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of the kingdom in the hand of thy God (Isaiah 62). And they that approach, etc. As if to say: Let those who did not hear Christ teaching in the flesh not be saddened as though deceived by men. Christ speaks through the mouth of the saints; through the feet the teaching of the head is heard; whence: He that heareth you, heareth me, etc. (Luke 10). Or those approach his feet to take in doctrine who, burning with spiritual desire, watch day and night over the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures. But because these things were said of the New Testament, there follows, in the voice of those through whom Moses speaks, about the old law: He commanded us a law, etc.
33.4: 33.4 The inheritance. Because this is the usefulness of the law, the inheritance of Abraham promised: If you be willing, and will hearken to me, you shall eat the good things of the land. He shall be with the most upright, etc. Jacob, blessed by the angel, was called Israel, that is, upright of God; and the Jew converted to the faith, blessed after the resurrection by him whom in the passion he prevailed over, is called most upright for the profession of justice. Whence: Hear, Jacob my servant, and thou most upright whom I have chosen, etc. (Isaiah 49).
33.5: 33.5 King. Christ. But I am appointed king by him, namely that he may make kingdom and power, who is king and the first power. With the tribes of Israel. Of whom the primitive Church. Well are the princes first named, then the tribes to be gathered, because the first were the apostles, and through them others believed.
33.6: 33.6 Let Reuben live. Having foretold the salvation of the primitive Church, he assigns to each tribe its own blessings; foretelling the true Israelites from both peoples, he prophesies now of Christ, now of the apostles, now of the primitive Church, now of the whole Church. Let Reuben live. As if to say: Although Reuben defiled his father's bed and lost the dignity of the firstborn, let him live nonetheless, and, doing penance, not die. The sons of Reuben, that is, the Jews signified by Reuben, defiled the Father's bed, that is, defiled Christ his Son with unclean spittle: yet they are reserved for penance, but few in number compared with the Church of the Gentiles. Reuben. Son of vision, because the mother said (Genesis 29): The Lord hath seen my affliction. This is the firstborn, signifying the elect from the Jews, who, dead by denying and crucifying Christ, converted by the preaching of the apostles, have been given life by faith in Christ: these are sons of vision, because saved by regard of divine mercy.
33.7: 33.7 This is for Judah. Judah, which is interpreted confession, signifies the universal Church, in which is confession of divine praise and thanksgiving. Of whom the mother says: Now will I praise the Lord (Genesis 29). This is the true bride of Christ, who, adorned with the necklaces of virtues, is not proud but gives thanks; for her he prays that he may be heard. Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah. Namely of the kings who came from Judah, who desired Christ; and of Christ himself, who says: I confess to thee, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, etc. (Luke 10). Hands. He prayed to the Lord for Judah, to whom now he promises the Lord's help, as though Judah should not presume on his own strength but trust in him who says: Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world (John 16); whose hands on the cross fought against spiritual wickednesses, that through death he might destroy him who had the empire of death. Helper. That he may conquer and say: Upon my high places he, the conqueror, will lead me (Habakkuk 3): for he himself conquers in us, and for his victory crowns us in mercy and compassion.
33.8: 33.8 Perfection. As if to say: how perfect you are, and how holy is your teaching, you have declared through Moses. Or: from your holy man, that is, the Levites, is your perfection and your doctrine. For they must keep the law, do it and teach it. Thy perfection. These things are said to the choir of angels and martyrs and of all the perfect, who fulfilled the perfection of charity by dying for the Lord; and, renouncing the world, attained the summit of ecclesiastical teaching, like true Levites having no portion on earth, but saying with the Prophet: The Lord is the portion of my inheritance, etc. (Psalm 15); according to that: If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, etc. (Luke 9). He that shall lose his life for me, etc. (Matthew 10). But Christ is the true Levi, who did and taught all these things. The Levites themselves cling to him, imitating him even to blood, of whose passion is added: Whom thou hast proved in the temptation, etc. At the waters. It is the place where he refused Moses and Aaron entrance into the promised land. At the waters. It signifies the law, which refused entrance into the heavenly kingdom to those living badly. The waters: the peoples, who in contradiction cried out: Crucify him. His blood be upon us, and upon our children (Matthew 27). To the crown of perfection he joins Levi:
33.9: 33.9 Who hath said to his father. When they made the golden calf, at Moses' command the Levites, girded with swords, slew the idolaters from gate to gate. In avenging idolatry they did not recognize their own, because they killed without distinction. Whence: If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, he cannot be my disciple (Luke 14, 18). Who said to his father and mother, etc. We ought also, in temporal matters, to benefit most those to whom we are more closely joined. We ought to acknowledge the bond of earthly kinship; but if it hinders the course of the mind, to ignore it, so that affection fills the inward parts of the mind but does not turn it from the spiritual purpose. The cows signify this well, who under the ark of the Lord, going toward the hills, walked with affection and a firm mind: going on, they lowed for their calves, but, having taken the road, did not turn their steps aside.
33.10: 33.10 They shall put incense. As Aaron, standing between the dead and the living, made supplication for the people. They shall put incense. The prayer of the saints is a most sweet incense to the Lord: when the people sins, the fury of the Lord is mitigated by it, because, purified from all earthly filth, kindled with heavenly desire, it burns like incense in the sight of God, and like a holocaust from the altar of a pious heart the flame of devotion flies up to heaven. This fits especially the apostles and martyrs, of whom it is said: As gold in the furnace he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust he hath received them (Wisdom 3).
33.11: 33.11 Receive. As if grateful, that thou mayest reward. White robes are now given to each, namely the gladness of souls; and in the judgment, with immortality received in the body, they will shine as the sun and run to and fro like sparks among the reeds, namely consuming the empty and unfruitful adversaries; of whose punishment is added: Strike the backs. As if to say: they thought they were shedding the blood of the martyrs with impunity, but as it were behind their back an unforeseen punishment was being prepared, that is, eternal damnation, into which falling they will not be able to rise. Whence: A rod for the back of the imprudent (Proverbs 26).
33.12: 33.12 And Benjamin.
