He seems to allude to the history, because Jacob, a patriarch and prophet full of the Spirit, loved Benjamin uniquely, and by the dispensation of God the place devoted to divine worship was decreed to be guarded by his tribe; whence he adds: As in a bridal chamber all the day, etc. Most beloved. Christ is the most beloved of God the Father, who says of himself: This is my beloved Son (Matthew 17). He dwells confidently at the right hand of the Father, to whom it is said: Sit thou at my right hand (Psalm 109). Otherwise: Benjamin, from son of sorrow called son of the right hand, expresses Paul, who from persecutor became an apostle and vessel of election: he himself was of this tribe; and it was fitting that as the forerunner of the Lord was foretold by prophetic oracle, so the master of the Gentiles, about to profit the whole world, should be proclaimed among the great mysteries of the Church. In his mind Christ dwelt with confidence, when amid countless dangers he constantly preached him before Gentiles and kings. Of whose soul it is said: As in a bridal chamber he shall dwell all the day. Or enjoying with wondrous delight a marital union, and fruitful with the offspring of virtues, leaving the secret of his most peaceful heart to no unrest of any vice; or, dwelling in it as in a bridal chamber, like a beautiful bridegroom, he joins to his embraces through his preaching the virgin minds of believers. Whence: After her shall virgins be brought to the king (Psalm 43). He himself also says: For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Corinthians 11). The divinity also dwells confidently in the humanity of Christ. He shall dwell in the bridal chamber signifies that in the womb of the Virgin the Church was joined to the heavenly bridegroom, and rests confidently in the strength of Christ's power and in works. And he shall rest between his shoulders. Burdens are carried on the shoulders, therefore in them robust patience is designated. And Christ rested in him all the more willingly the more hard labours he bore for him: he embraced him the more closely the more he was torn from his embrace by no terror. Whence he says: Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? (Romans 8).
33.13: 33.13 And to Joseph he said. Joseph is interpreted increased. This is Christ, who, cast off by the Jews his brethren, became prince in the Egypt of this age, and freed the human race from the want of famine by the distribution of the wheat of the Gospel: who is truly the Saviour of the world. Of the blessing of the Lord be his land. Literally it signifies fertility, which the two tribes from Joseph, that is, Ephraim and Manasseh, had in abundance of crops, fruits and pasture of cattle. This is Bashan, a most fertile region, whence it is interpreted fatness. By the temperate climate of the sky, and by the dew, the fruit, and the abundance of springs and rivers, which are signified in the deep, man is delighted. Thou hast blessed, O Lord, thy land, namely the Church, which is filled with the blessing of virtues not by her own virtue but divinely. Whence: Blessed be God, who hath blessed us with spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ (Ephesians 1). Heavens. The apostles and evangelists are called heaven on account of the unity of faith and doctrine, of whom elsewhere it is said in the plural: The heavens shew forth the glory of God, etc. (Psalm 18). For in them, shining in life and contemplation, as in heaven God dwells, thundering terror, raining consolation, and flashing with miracles. Dew. Heavenly preaching, of wondrous subtlety and grace, by which hearts are watered against the heat of temptation, and that they may be ever green with virtues; whence: God give thee of the dew of heaven, etc. (Genesis 27). The deep, that is, so that it may become richer, watered by a rising spring like the paradise of God. Whence: A fountain went up out of the earth, watering all the surface of the earth (Genesis 2). From the sea his sense abounded, and his thoughts from the great deep. For in vain does the teacher's word water outwardly, unless the grace of the Creator waters inwardly. Whence he adds: Of the fruits of the hills, etc.
33.14: 33.14 Of the sun. Of Christ, who is the sun of justice, who says: The just shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matthew 13), because we shall be like him. And of the moon. Of the Church, which receives these fruits from the sun, that is, from Christ: let her therefore always look upon the sun with full devotion, lest at some time turning away she lose the light.
33.15: 33.15 Of the fruits of the eternal hills. The eternal hills are the faithful of the Old Testament, humble sons, founded with immovable firmness in the faith of the prophets and patriarchs, whence: The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills (Isaiah 2), by whose fruits the land of Joseph is blessed, when the Church of Christ bears fruit in faith by the doctrine of prophecy and the example of virtue. And it is to be noted that above, in the fruits and dew of heaven the evangelical teaching is signified, here in the top of the ancient mountains and the fruits of the eternal hills the legal and prophetic, and with both the land of Joseph is enriched; because the holy Church is formed by the pages of both Testaments and the examples of the new and old Fathers; whence: All fruits, new and old, my beloved, I have kept for thee (Canticles 7), and: Every scribe instructed bringeth forth out of his treasure new things and old (Matthew 13). The Manichaeans and Jews, therefore, because the former do not receive the Old Testament and the latter the New, cannot inherit in this rich land.
33.16: 33.16 And of the fruits. The Church throughout the whole world, fruitful in the fruit of justice and the largess of gifts, has received from the fullness of her Joseph; whence follows: The blessing of him that appeared. The whole Joseph, that is, head and body, full of blessing, but the fullness of the blessing especially in the head; whence: Like the precious ointment on the head, that ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, etc. (Psalm 32). He, preeminent by the privilege of grace over his brethren, that is, the faithful, with the sevenfold Spirit, like the true Samson, a Nazarite from the womb of the virgin, that is, consecrated to God, shone as with seven locks untouched. Upon the head of Joseph, of Christ, who is the head of the Church, in whom all nations are blessed, of whose passion and resurrection is added: As the firstborn of a bull, etc. As. AUGUSTINE, question 56. The firstborn of a bull is his beauty. It is not to be read so as to say the firstborn of a bull: but, since he is firstborn, his beauty is the beauty of a bull, on account of the horns of the cross. Christ, the fatted calf, whom from the herd of the fathers the Father sacrificed as firstborn when the Son returned, who on the third day was raised and appeared glorious, who is the firstborn from the dead and prince of the kings of the earth, after the glory of the resurrection adds horns from the power of the passion.
33.17: 33.17 Horns. He compares Joseph to the horns of the rhinoceros, signifying that Ephraim would hold the principate among the ten tribes, among whom Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim reigned in the time of Rehoboam son of Solomon. The horns of the rhinoceros. He signifies the horns of the cross, of which Habakkuk says: There is his strength hid (Habakkuk 3). For through infirmity of the flesh, like a ram, he is crowned with thorns by the mockers; he was caught by these horns, but by the incomparable strength of the passion he stood forth a unicorn, victor over death and over him who had the empire of death; whence: The weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1). He shall winnow. By the preaching of the cross separating chaff from wheat: for the word of the cross is foolishness to them that perish. Nations. Ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles, etc. (Psalm 2). For all these things are said of the inheritance of the true Joseph, which is the renowned land, and of its cultivators gathered from both peoples follows: These are the multitudes of Ephraim. These two tribes from Joseph are blessed not in themselves but in their parent. They signify the sons of both peoples, who are blessed in Christ according to that: In thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Genesis 22). The patriarch Jacob, blessing Ephraim and Manasseh with crossed hands in the manner of a cross, and preferring the younger to the firstborn, signified that they were to be blessed in the faith of the cross of Christ, in the younger from the Gentiles the faithful people, in Christ's grace younger in time but greater in faith: to which the grace of the Israelite people has passed, of whose inestimable multitude it is said: These are the multitudes, etc., whence: Many are the children of the desolate, more than of her that hath a husband (Isaiah 54). Manasseh, deprived of the honour of the firstborn and yet blessed, is the Jewish people, which in the greater part of itself was rejected for unbelief, yet in the remnant obtained the blessing, whence: Blindness in part has happened in Israel, etc. (Romans 11).
33.18: 33.18 And to Zebulun. Zebulun and Issachar received their portion in Galilee, where Christ taught most, whence he chose the apostles. By them, then, the apostles are designated, and joy is promised them in their going out, because going out from their borders they subjected the people of the Gentiles to Christ, and in tents for the conversion of the Jews, from whom they themselves were chosen. For both peoples, then, present joy is promised them and future: because in the present they rejoiced at their conversion, and in heaven they are rewarded with eternal joy. In tents, of the Jews, whence: May God enlarge Japheth, and dwell in the tents of Shem (Genesis 9): because in the churches the breadth of the lesser people dwells among the Jews by unity of faith.
33.19: 33.19 To the mountain. Zion, namely, or Jerusalem, or contemplation and height of virtues. They shall call. Teaching that justice is only in the faith of Christ. For Christ is the end of the law unto justice to everyone that believeth (Romans 10). On the mountain they sacrifice victims of justice, while they teach that all who come to Christ, on whom the Church is built, are justified not by works of the law but by faith in Christ, according to that: The just shall live by faith (Habakkuk 1). True Christians, then, are the victims of justice, which are sacrificed by the apostles, while they are taught to mortify earthly desires that spiritual things may be given life; whence: If by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live (Romans 8). There they shall sacrifice. There is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, which is placed upon this mountain. Who shall suck the abundance of the sea. These tribes were devoted to three kinds of commerce, bringing back merchandise from regions overseas, and hidden treasures, silver, namely, gold or gems, they will suck like milk, that is, easily receive. Who shall suck the abundance of the sea. It signifies the calling of the Gentiles. For the sea signifies the whole human race; whence: The kingdom of heaven is like to a net cast into the sea, and gathering of all kind of fishes (Matthew 13). The sea is the world, the net the teaching, every kind of fishes every sex, age and condition. The apostles therefore sucked the abundance of the sea like milk, because they drew the crowds of peoples flowing together to the teaching of the Gospel to the increase of the body of Christ. Hidden. The Lord knoweth who are his (2 Timothy 2). For many are called, but few chosen (Matthew 20). Sands: the multitude of unbelievers; treasures: the precious souls of the elect. So they sucked, that of those who heard the Gospel, some, like vessels unto honour, were transferred to the treasures of the king, others, like barren and useless sands, remained empty.
33.20: 33.20 And to Gad he said. In the blessing of Gad he seems to foretell the power of strong men, or judgment, who came from that tribe, like Jephthah and many others. In the breadth. Because all the fullness of the blessing rested upon Christ, whence he blessed his own. Gad. That is, girded, signifies Christ, who, about to fight against spiritual wickednesses, appeared girded with the power of divinity in the infirmity of the flesh, according to that: The Lord is clothed with strength and hath girded himself (Psalm 112). And elsewhere: The Lord strong and mighty, mighty in battle, etc. He is blessed in the breadth, because he received a most ample kingdom not among the Jews alone but among all nations. Hence the Prophecy says: From the rising of the sun to the going down, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise. But because he came to this glory through the humility of the passion, of his death he adds: He rested as a lion. I have power to lay down my life (John 10). The power of death, not the necessity, is expressed; whence: No man taketh it away from me, but I lay it down of myself. Ibid. As a lion he roared. For whatever he said he fulfilled powerfully. And he took the arm and the top of the head. When rising from the dead he subjected to himself the strength of enemies. He took also the top of the head, that is, he bowed the loftiness of worldly empire to receive the faith; whence: And all kings of the earth shall adore him; all nations shall serve him (Psalm 71). There follows the new state of his kingdom.
33.21: 33.21 And he saw his principality, that in his part. With kingdoms and nations subjected to him, his power appeared, not by the terror of arms but by the power of teaching. Laid up. Hidden, while he writes his laws in the hearts of the faithful; whence he says: You have the unction from the Holy One, and you need not that any man teach you; but as his unction teacheth you of all things (1 John 2). Or, Laid up, because in the law and the prophets he lay hidden in figures, and taught hidden what he declared openly in the Gospel; whence: Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded to them (Luke 24). Who was with the princes of the people. As helper, whence: The Lord working with them, and confirming the word with signs that followed (Mark 16), because he says: Without me you can do nothing (John 15). He did justices. That is, justifying those who believe in him, and at last he will judge according to merits with Israel, that is, with his people chosen for the vision of God. Justices. The justifications of believers. For he justifies the ungodly by faith. For by the works of the law no flesh shall be justified.
33.22: 33.22 Of Dan also. Others think Antichrist is signified by Dan, whom they suppose will be born of this tribe: he is the lion's whelp, that is, of the devil, who will flow abundantly from Bashan, because full of confusion; for Bashan is interpreted confusion, or fatness, or locust. Dan is also judgment, Bashan shame. But Dan signifies Christ, who says: For judgment I am come into this world (John 9). Lion's whelp on account of strength, and because he deigned to become a little one; but taking on our infirmity, he did not lose his power, for the weakness of God is stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1). Of him it is said: The lion of the tribe of Juda hath prevailed, etc. (Apocalypse 5). He bore the shame of the cross from the Jews, who thought his name would be blotted out by death: but he who through the infirmity of his flesh was a whelp in the passion appeared in the resurrection through the power of divinity an unconquered lion; whence the Apostle: Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13). As if therefore from Bashan he flowed abundantly, when through the shame of death coming to the glory of immortality, he watered the whole world with the streams of the Gospel; whence Isaiah: The earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the covering waters of the sea (Isaiah 2). Dan a lion's whelp. This he says on account of Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan, and was like a strong lion, whose possession extended to Bashan. But Antichrist will flow abundantly from Bashan, because he will be filled with the fatness of luxury and of all vices. He shall possess the sea and the south. Because his possession reaches from the southern part westward as far as the Tyrrhenian sea. He shall possess the sea and the south. For through the apostles the Church from Jews and Gentiles is acquired for Christ. By the western sea, which is understood here, the Jews are figured, who serve the shadow and the copy, and have not the light of knowledge and truth, and because the sun of justice has set for them, they have remained in perpetual darkness. The apostles possessed this west when they subjected to Christ very many of them illuminated by the grace of faith, that those who were once darkness might be light in the Lord. In the south is understood the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, the veil of the law being removed, enjoys the light of the Gospel, and, lying down with the bridegroom at noon, contemplates the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.
33.24: 33.24 Of Asher also he said: Blessed in children be Asher, let him be acceptable to his brethren. Asher is blessed, Christ, namely, the hope of our blessedness, whose firstfruits he showed us by rising from the dead. He is blessed in children, because believers, reborn by his grace, have filled the whole world with his likeness, to whom it is said: Believe in the light, that you may be the children of light (John 12). They bear the fruit of light in all goodness and justice and truth. This came about because he was pleasing by true charity to his brethren, that is, the apostles, whom he chose from Judea, so that, spurning the figures, they might rejoice in the truth of the Gospel, and because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus. And whence did they have such abundance of charity? he adds: Let him dip his foot in oil, etc. And let him dip his foot in oil. Christ, our head, ascending into heaven, anointed most copiously with the oil of the Holy Spirit the apostles, namely his feet, who were to go round the world preaching while still remaining on earth, so that they might fail through no labour but be strong in the clarity of unfading joy. He also supplied the incorruptible protection of the shoe, of which is added: Iron and brass shall be thy shoe. GREGORY, Morals, book 34, chapter 5. This of the Church, etc., until with these shoes the true pasch is to be celebrated.
33.25: 33.25 As the days of youth. It signifies that this tribe abounded in prosperity and delights until the old age of captivity. As. To the Church is promised a vigorous and green old age: that as she strongly overcame all assaults at the beginning, so, as the end approaches, she may overcome the fury of Antichrist, whence: Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world (Matthew 28). And elsewhere: My old age in plentiful mercy (Psalm 91).
33.26: 33.26 There is no God. Marvelling at the aforesaid in praise of Christ, who did all these things, he bursts forth rejoicing. The rider of heaven. By his own power he ascended, and daily draws the Church to himself. Draw me, we will run after thee to the odour of thy ointments (Canticles 1). The clouds. The apostles, who rain with words and flash with miracles: whom, ascending into heaven, he sent to preach; whence: The clouds poured out their voice (Psalm 76), which run to and fro with no one delaying, working signs and wonders not by their own but by Christ's power, and, as with lightning flashes, terrifying the hearts of mortals, whence: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course (2 Timothy 4).
33.27: 33.27 His dwelling is above, etc. The body raised from the dead and placed at the right hand of the Father, of which it is said: Destroy this temple (John 2). The arms. The power, namely, of the passion, which defends all, which he received on the cross with arms outstretched. Under the arms. These arms, that is, defend those fighting against the true Amalek: nor are they weighed down by weariness as Moses's were, but sustain with unwearied power until they gain the true victory. Let us therefore venerate in the heights the firstfruits of our resurrection, and in the depths the sacrament of our redemption, so that we too, the adversary having been conquered, may attain the glory of immortality, of which to the true Israel it is promised: He shall cast out the enemy from before thee. And alone. Living, namely, by his own manner and his own laws, whence Balaam: The people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations (Numbers 23).
33.28: 33.28 The eye of Jacob. He who here toiled at supplanting vices, there will behold, with the lightest glance of mind, unceasingly the glory of Christ, who for us took the earth of true flesh: so that he who here was fed by his body and blood through the sacrament of wheat and wine, there may be fattened by the perpetual vision of his divinity, whence: I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear (Psalm 16). And elsewhere: I will manifest myself to him (John 14). Then Jacob, turned into perfect Israel, will see God face to face, with so ample, so subtle, so delightful a knowledge of God, as if filled with the lightest dew, that the knowledge of the preachers by which we are now instructed will seem to grow dim; whence: Whether knowledge shall be destroyed (1 Corinthians 13). And elsewhere: Dark water in the clouds of the air, from the brightness in his sight (Psalm 17), to which when it is attained, all this teaching will cease, and all shall be taught of God (John 6); hence he fittingly adds: Happy art thou, O Israel, etc. And the heavens shall grow dark, as if so abundantly the dew for making the earth fruitful will be poured out that the gaze of men grows dim. In this it is signified that the Jews, when they loved earthly wealth beyond measure, grew dim and could not recognize Christ; whence: If we let him alone so, all will believe in him, etc.
33.29: 33.29 Who is like to thee, O people? As if to say: therefore blessed, therefore none like thee, because you hope for salvation not from your own power but from the grace of Christ, who saves his people from their sins. And the sword of thy glory. In the future striking adversaries with irrevocable severity, when he will avenge the blood of his servants. The sword is here now hidden in the humility of the suffering, in the glory of the risen it will be revealed, therefore it is called the sword of the glory of Israel. Christ therefore protects the one fighting like a shield, and will avenge the one triumphing like a sword of glory. To him as to the head, at the end of the prophecy the glory of the body is referred, when it is said: They shall deny thee. They will abominate and hate, like Balak, who asked Balaam to drive back the Israelites by cursing. Thou shalt tread. By subjecting them to the Church, which they abominate and persecute. It is to be noted that there are only eleven blessings. For Simeon is not found in these blessings, in which Judas is excluded by the apostles, eleven alone remaining. For this reason also the children of Israel came from Horeb in eleven encampments to the place where they received Deuteronomy.
34.1: 34.1 Moses therefore went up. Both Moses and the other fathers of the Old Testament, raised by the spirit to the height of contemplation, could foresee the grace of the New Testament, which was given in Christ, both in the conferring of virtues and in the receiving of the heavenly kingdom: but they could not await it in the flesh, and died in faith and hope, led down to the underworld, where they awaited the coming of the Redeemer, who through the blood of his redemption would free them from there. And the Lord shewed him. Moses saw the promised land and did not enter, because the law presignified by words and figures the coming of Christ and the teaching of the Gospel, but led no one to perfection.
34.2: 34.2 All the land. Part of the whole land, which he could see from the very high mountain. Or he showed him all the land in the spirit.
34.5: 34.5 And Moses died there, etc. God spares none of the elect, and punishes even the smallest sins even in his friends; whence: Moses and Aaron among his priests, and he added: Thou wast a merciful God to them, taking vengeance on all their inventions. The law, namely, being ended, which served the Lord in its time, the city destroyed and the altar, nowhere sacrifices, nowhere libations, nowhere priest or high priest.
34.6: 34.6 In the valley. He died on the mountain, was buried in the valley, because the law was glorious in its time: but compared with the Gospel it seems hidden and lowly; whence: I gave them precepts that were not good. And no man hath known. The Jews suppose this was done lest the Jews, always prone to idolatry, should worship the dead man as God; but according to allegory it signifies that the time and manner of ending the law are hidden in God's foreknowledge alone, and that neither the depth of the wisdom of God nor the secret of his counsel is open to anyone, because his judgments are incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable.
34.7: 34.7 Moses was a hundred and twenty years old. If you add the sums of single numbers from one up to fifteen in natural order, namely one and two and three, and so on, it makes a hundred and twenty. Fifteen is made of seven and eight; seven refers to the sabbath, eight to circumcision, because the boy was circumcised on the eighth day. If you look to the New Testament, you have the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and in the eighth the resurrection of Christ; a hundred and twenty therefore signifies those who strive, even in the Old Testament, to fulfil the precepts of the Law and the Gospel. Moses was a hundred and twenty years old. This signifies that both he and the other fathers of the Old Testament, after the perfection of the commandments of God, which is in the two precepts of charity, are fit, through the grace of Christ and the redemption of his blood, for eternal rest and the life to come; whose eye was not dim, that is, the gaze of their pious intention was not obscured by cloud, nor were the teeth of malice moved, because their order of discretion was not disturbed by the tempest of vices; the hundred and twenty years of the lawgiver is the number by which the height of Solomon's temple was confirmed. The primitive Church also, after the passion and resurrection and ascension of the Lord, received the grace of the Holy Spirit with this number of men. For fifteen, which is composed of seven and eight, signifies the future life which is now borne in the sabbath of souls and will be perfected in the resurrection of bodies. Fifteen also, drawn into a triangle, that is, counted with its parts, makes a hundred and twenty. Aptly therefore the blessedness of the elect in the future life is signified by one hundred and twenty, and the third upper room of the house of God is completed, because after the labours of the faithful, after the rest of souls, the full happiness of the Church will be completed in the glory of the resurrection.
34.8: 34.8 And they wept. Because death reigned even over those who had not sinned, from Adam until Moses: therefore tears follow him descending to the underworld. JEROME, letter to Paula. It is no wonder if Moses and Aaron, etc., until but within, that is, to serve the will of the Lord. And were completed. From this the custom seems to have arisen that for the faithful dead the offices of piety be paid for thirty days.
34.9: 34.9 Laid upon him. In his Scriptures he bore witness to him, saying: God will raise up a prophet, etc. (Deuteronomy 18), whence: If you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also (John 5).
34.10: 34.10 And there arose not, etc. This, it is said, Ezra added of his own, who with divine insight restored the library burned by the Chaldeans, and invented the letters which the Jews now use, whence he was also called a ready scribe. And there arose not a prophet. Because Moses was more excellent than all the prophets of the Old Testament: whence the Jews arrogantly say: We are the disciples of Moses (John 9). But after the Lord of the prophets came incarnate into the world, all that former dignity and shadow of things to come ceased: because the law and the figure were given by Moses; grace and truth came by Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law unto justice to everyone that believeth (Hebrews 10; John 1; Romans 10). And he buried him in the valley. Namely the Lord. And by this is signified that, the impediment of nature being removed through Christ, the pure soul, separated, ascends to God: and the body, which is buried in the earth, remains until the judgment. Ecclesiastes 12: Until the dust return into its earth, from whence it was, and the spirit return to God, who gave it. May he grant us this prosperous return, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
1.22: 1.22 And you came to me. In the book of Numbers it is written that the Lord told Moses to send men to view the land; here, however, the people are read to have said: Let us send men to view the land. But the people first suggested this to Moses, Moses referred it to the Lord, and according to his command he afterwards sent the spies.
1.23: 1.23 I sent of you. ISIDORE. The twelve spies sent to explore the fertile land, etc., until for neither is Christ without the law, nor the law without Christ. Twelve. These signify the teachers of the Church, of whom some by teaching perverse things lead the people astray, others by preaching right things bring progress.
1.33: 1.33 Showing by night. The night is the sinner, the day the life of the just. In the pillar of fire is the damnation of the wicked, to whom the Lord will appear terrible in judgment; in the pillar of cloud, the light and gentle vision by which the elect will be consoled. By day, by a pillar. Overshadowing in the heat of this age, and sustaining by the strength and propitiation of his flesh.
1.34: 1.34 He swore. God is not subject to passions, nor to the fault of anger. But through these things the love of Moses toward the people is made manifest, and the goodness of God, which surpasses all understanding.
1.35: 1.35 No one shall see. A similar thing is said of those who, invited to the supper, excused themselves: None of those men that were invited shall taste of my supper (Luke 14). The worst generation does not possess the good land, because it does not believe in the incarnation of Christ.
1.37: 1.37 Nor to be wondered at. Here Moses says that, on account of the people, the Lord was angry with him and said that he would not enter the promised land, whereas in the book of Numbers it is read: The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Because you have not believed me, to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these peoples into the land which I will give them. But the following statement seems to resolve the question: This, it says, is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel strove with words against the Lord, etc. (Numbers 20). For the strife and rebellion of the people was the cause of the anger and vengeance, both on the people and on Moses and Aaron. Neither shalt thou enter. ISIDORE. It seems that in Miriam, etc., until when Christ is recognized as lofty like the eminence of a mountain.
1.41: 1.41 And when you were armed. This sentence strikes human pride, which presumes upon its own strength and does not trust in the power of God. For the Amorites, that is, the embittering ones, are spiritual enemies who dwell on the mountains of pride and slay the presumptuous, from Seir to Hormah, that is, from the squalor of vices to the damnation of punishments: for Seir is interpreted hairy, Hormah anathema. For whoever does not fear to be defiled by the filth of vices, him it is necessary, according to his deserts, to be handed over to the fires of Gehenna. For demons wish to entangle us in earthly desires, and if we persevere in sins and do not cease to climb the mountain of pride, they cut us down with fiery darts and bring us to perpetual anathema. Therefore, not as the Pelagians would have it, let us not presume on our own power, but, considering our weakness, let us obey the Lord in all things, so that, the enemies overcome, we may obtain the promised joys of the heavenly homeland. We must beware lest, murmuring against the Lord, we climb the mountain of pride, thinking we can be saved by our own strength, lest we be at once handed over to the Amorites, that is, to demons.
2.1: 2.1 And we went round Mount Seir, etc. Seir is a mountain in the land of Edom, on which Esau dwelt in the region of Gabalene, where the Horite had dwelt before, whom Chedorlaomer slew; it received the name Seir, that is, hairy, from Esau, who was hairy and rough. The Horites, like the other nations which they overcame, who descended from the seed of the patriarchs, express wicked spirits or vices, which can be overcome by those who follow the footsteps and teachings of the holy Fathers and wage spiritual warfare under Christ the king, of which it is said: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, etc. (Ephesians 6).
2.9: 2.9 I have given to the children of Lot. Ar is the metropolis of the Moabites, on the bank of the torrent Arnon: formerly possessed by the very ancient nation of the Emim, afterwards held by the children of Lot, that is, the Moabites, the inhabitants having been overthrown. It is shown today on the summit of a mountain, but the torrent, descending through precipices, flows into the Dead Sea. Ar is interpreted he has raised up; Emim, that is, terrible ones: these are the demons, who stir up strife and contentions and prepare the darts of wickedness against the faithful. The Anakim also, begotten of the stock of Anak and equal to giants in stature, signify according to their name demons, for they are interpreted as a necklace on a lofty neck. For, lifted up by the pride of arrogance, they ascribe all the equipment of their warfare to their own strength, and so they easily yield to those who trust in the power of God and say with the Psalmist: The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he is become my salvation (Psalm 117).
2.14: 2.14 From Kadesh-barnea. JEROME, letter to Fabiola. Kadesh-barnea is a place in the desert, adjoining the city of Petra in Arabia, where Miriam died and Moses, striking the rock, gave water to the thirsty people. The tomb of Miriam is still shown there today, and the princes of Amalek too were slain there by Chedorlaomer.
2.26: 2.26 So I sent messengers, etc. Sihon signifies the devil, which is a useless seed, or a fruitless tree, or one lifted up. Israel, the Christian people, who desire to pass through the way of this world and come to the heavenly kingdoms. Here he sends to Sihon with words of peace, promising that he will not dwell in his land but only pass through, and will walk by the king's highway. Everyone promised this when he first came to the water of baptism and received the first seals of faith. For he renounced the devil, and his pomps, and his works, and all his service, and his pleasures. This is what is said: Israel will not turn aside into his field, or into his vineyard, and will not drink water from his well (Numbers 21), that is, he will no longer take up the discipline either of astrology or of magic, or of any teaching that is against piety: but he will drink from the springs of the Saviour, he will not forsake the fountain of living water to drink from the fountain of Sihon, but will walk by the king's highway, which is Christ, who says: I am the way, the truth, and the life (John 14), and the king, according to that: Give to the king thy judgment, O God (Psalm 71). He will not turn aside into his field or into his vineyard, that is, to his works, or to his perverse senses. The Amorites are interpreted speaking ones, or embittering ones, because they provoke God to bitterness and trust only in words, such as poets, astrologers, philosophers, who speak vain things; but the kingdom of God is not in speech, but in power. The faithful wish to pass through in peace and to be peaceable even with the enemies of peace: but they offend the prince of the world the more, the more they say they do not wish to stay with him or touch anything of his. Thence, the more embittered, he persecutes, stirs up dangers, threatens torments, gathers his people, and goes out to fight against Israel: his people are the princes and judges of the world, and all the ministers of wickedness who persecute the people of God: but he too comes to Jahaz, which is interpreted fulfilment of the command. For whoever comes to the fulfilment of God's commandments will not fear Sihon or his raging army. For to fulfil God's commandments is to overcome the devil and his army. Thus God crushes Satan under our feet, and gives us power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy.
2.30: 2.30 Because he had hardened. Long patience, by not correcting; whence in Exodus: I have hardened the heart of Pharaoh (Exodus 10); and the Psalmist: He turned their heart, that they should hate his people (Psalm 104). The cause of the hardening is added, that he might be delivered into your hands, that is, that he might be crushed by you; which would not happen unless he resisted, nor would he resist unless he were hardened. If we seek the justice of this matter, his judgments are unsearchable, but there is no iniquity with God.
2.33: 2.33 And we struck him. Those who are true Israelites, not Jews in the flesh but in the spirit, dwell in all the cities of the Amorites, when the Churches of Christ are propagated throughout the whole world, and each one of us was a city of king Sihon: because folly, pride, impiety, and everything the devil suggests reigned in us. But when the strong one was conquered and his vessels plundered, we became cities of Israel, the inheritance of the saints, the fruitless tree having first been cut down, the proud king cast out, and the meek one reigning in us, who says: Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart, etc. (Matthew 11). The names of the places agree too: Aroer is interpreted raising up; Arnon, heap of sorrow; Gilead, heap of witness. From Aroer, therefore, which is on the bank of the torrent Arnon, etc. Because every person of whatever dignity, trusting in the arrogance of pride or in worldly pomp, together with the persecutors who afflict Christians with various tribulations, even up to the assemblies of heretics, who fight against the Church with depraved testimonies of the Scriptures but cannot resist, are handed over, conquered, into the hands of the saints along with their dwellings.
3.1: 3.1 And so turning. Against Og, who is king of Bashan, they do not deign to send ambassadors, nor to ask passage through his land: they immediately fight with him, overcoming him and his people. Bashan is interpreted shame: rightly, therefore, no ambassadors are sent to this nation, nor is passage asked; for there ought to be no passage for us, nor ascent, to shame, which must at once be fought down and wholly avoided. Og is interpreted closing; he signifies carnal things, by desire for which the soul is shut out and separated from God. Against these we must so wage war that no vice is left. For none ought to be left in the kingdom of shame; shameful things must be cut away so that honourable and religious things can be built. In the kingdom of Sihon or Moab this is not commanded. For perhaps we have need of something from them, which the manifold use of the present life requires: otherwise we would have to go out of this world. But from Bashan, that is, from shame, we leave nothing, because we need nothing of it. And what is shameful cannot be honourable.
3.4: 3.4 Sixty. It confirms the sense above. For the number sixty, like six, signifies perfection. Well does it record sixty cities laid waste in the region of Og king of Bashan, that is, of the devil, who is king of shame; because it signifies that the delight in all vices must be destroyed perfectly. Argob, that is, accursed loftiness, signifies earthly pride, which reigns in the children of wrath: the cities being destroyed, it says men and women and little ones were slain, and the beasts and spoils plundered, because, the stronghold of the devil overcome, whatever in our flesh we sense as rebellious, whatever wanton along with childish thoughts, must be crushed by zeal for God; but whatever we find fit for the service of God, in the simplicity of a pure mind or in the adornment of the members, we ought to keep.
3.12: 3.12 And the land. GREGORY, Morals, book 27, chapter 10. There are many in the Church, etc., until namely vain desires and irrational motions of the mind. Reuben and Gad. RABANUS. Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob, etc., until but with the women themselves and the little ones they strive to cross over and reach the homeland.
3.28: 3.28 Command Joshua, etc. It was done by a great dispensation of God that Moses, who is the type of the law, should not bring the people into the promised land, because the law brought no one to perfection; Joshua, however, is the type of Christ, which is interpreted saviour. For Christ saved his people, and fittingly as leader and prince brought them into the promised land.
4.1: 4.1 And now, Israel, hear the precepts and judgments. You shall not add. He teaches the rule of equity, and strikes down every heresy. For he forbids adding anything of wicked intent to right doctrine, or taking away anything of the truth: for we must walk by the king's highway, not to the right or to the left; whence: For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them (Hosea 14). Likewise John says: If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book; if any man shall take away, God shall take away his part out of the book of life (Apocalypse 22).
4.7: 4.7 Neither is there another, etc. There is no other nation so great, namely in the dignity of gifts, not in the multitude of peoples. For the nation of the Jews did not surpass other nations in number or power, but by the prerogative of the fathers and divine favour.
4.9: 4.9 Which they saw. Sight holds the primacy among all the senses: therefore it is put for every sense.
4.16: 4.16 A graven likeness. AUGUSTINE, question 4 on Deuteronomy. Perhaps by these two words he signified one thing, etc., until which is customary concerning men.
4.18: 4.18 That is under. AUGUSTINE, question 5. Whether he wished water to be understood as earth, etc., until and could not have earthly animals.
4.19: 4.19 Which he created. AUGUSTINE, question 6. It was not said in such a way, etc., until but not the worship which other nations have.
4.23: 4.23 A graven likeness. AUGUSTINE, question 7. Here, speaking generally, he put likeness and passed over image in silence, because if there is no likeness, there is no image either.
4.26: 4.26 I call heaven and earth to witness this day, etc. By that which contains he signifies that which is contained.
4.30: 4.30 But in the latter. He foretells the conversion of Israel to the faith of Christ, so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, all Israel may be saved.
4.32: 4.32 From the highest heaven. AUGUSTINE, question 8. Why he did not say likewise from the highest part of the earth, etc., until since this is said of the final gathering of the elect.
5.1: 5.1 Hear, O Israel, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 9 on Deuteronomy. Whether it was said for this reason, etc., until and to see, and to hear, and to retain in memory?
5.4: 5.4 Face to face, etc. AUGUSTINE. A little before, he took care to admonish, etc., until although some have hoped for this.
5.5: 5.5 Between you and God. The same, question 10. As though the Lord were in a place, etc., until hearing from the midst of the fire the voice of God speaking the decalogue of the law.
5.9: 5.9 Repaying iniquity, etc. ISIDORE. There are those who explain thus, etc., until but let him long defer his sentence. To those who hate me, and showing mercy to many thousands that love me, etc. That is, to those who hate the Lord by hereditary impiety. For it is perverse that the sins of the fathers should be imputed to sons who do not sin, since it was said through Ezekiel: The son shall not bear the iniquity, etc. (Ezekiel 18).
5.11: 5.11 You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, etc. The first commandment pertains to the Father, as is said in what follows: Hear, O Israel, the Lord thy God is one God (Deuteronomy 6); that is, hearing this you should worship one God the Father, not take up many gods. The second pertains to the Son, of whom it is said here: You shall not take the name of your God in vain, that is, do not reckon the Son of God to be a creature. For every creature is subject to vanity, but believe him equal to the Father, God of gods, God with God, through whom all things were made. The third pertains to the Spirit, by whose gift eternal rest is promised: for because the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold, therefore God sanctified the seventh day. For on the other days the sanctification of works is not named, except on the sabbath, on which God rested. Rightly, then, this commandment pertains to the Spirit: both on account of the name of sanctification, and on account of eternal rest, which belongs to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it is said thus: Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day: six days shalt thou labour, etc. In the work of six days, etc., the working of six thousand years seems to be signified, and in the seventh the time of eternal quiet, in which after good works eternal rest is promised. Whatever, then, we do, if we do it for the sake of the future rest, we keep the sabbath.
5.16: 5.16 Honour your father and your mother, as the Lord your God has commanded you. After the three commandments follow seven which pertain to the neighbour. Among the seven the first, but in the order of all the fourth, is: Honour thy father, etc. For from parents a man opens his eyes, and this life takes its beginning from their love: hence this commandment is called the greatest and first, namely on the other tablet. We are therefore commanded to honour our parents, and to show them the duty of piety and reverence; for he who does not do this to parents, how will he do it to others? The fifth: Thou shalt not commit adultery. That is, you shall not unite with anyone except a lawful wife. The sixth: Thou shalt not kill. He also kills who sees his neighbour dying of hunger or nakedness and does not help as far as he can. The seventh: Thou shalt not steal. In which he forbids all plunder. The eighth: Thou shalt not bear false witness. He abominates the crime of lying and falsehood. The ninth: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife. In which he also forbids adulterous thought. The tenth: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's goods. In which he strikes at ambition and concupiscence. The first, therefore, forbids stealthy intrusion; the second, error; the third, love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth, fornication; the sixth, cruelty; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth, falsehood; the ninth, the thought of adultery; the tenth, worldly cupidity. And it is to be noted that as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the people of God are ruled by ten commandments, and the demons are slain.
5.22: 5.22 In two tables of stone which he gave to me. ISIDORE. The two Testaments, etc., until namely the sensible and the intelligible.
5.29: 5.29 Who will grant them to have such a mind? God wishes it understood that this benefit is granted by his grace, so that in all things there may be the righteousness of God from faith, not as their own from the law; whence: I will take away the stony heart from them, and will give them a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36), that is, a heart with feeling, for flesh has feeling, but stone has none; and elsewhere: He hath made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not in the letter, but in the spirit.
6.5: 6.5 Thou shalt love the Lord. AUGUSTINE, On Christian Doctrine, book 1, chapters 26, 27, 28. Charity will not be taken away, etc., until who by reason of the opportunity of places and times or of any circumstances are more closely joined to us. GREGORY, Morals, book 7, chapter 10. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God, etc. Through the love of God the love of neighbour is begotten, etc., until for in good fortune a friend is not recognized, and in evil fortune an enemy is not hidden. The soul is of threefold nature: therefore it is commanded to love in three ways. God does not wish to share his love, so that we should love at once God and gold, or wife, or children. No man can serve two masters (Matthew 6); he is to be loved above all things, his love is put first.
6.8: 6.8 And thou shalt bind them as a sign. The Pharisees, interpreting this wrongly, wrote the decalogue, that is, the ten words, on little parchments, and wore them bound on the forehead. The Babylonians do this to this day, to be thought religious. Hence: For they enlarge their phylacteries, and make long their fringes (Matthew 23).
6.13: 6.13 And thou shalt swear by his name. AUGUSTINE, question 12. They are permitted to swear by the name of God, etc., until but he who does not swear at all is far from perjury.
6.16: 6.16 Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. He tempts God who, having something to do, commits himself without reason to danger, to test whether he can be delivered by God.
7.1: 7.1 Many nations. The seven nations are the seven principal vices, which the spiritual soldier, overcoming them by the grace of God, is commanded to exterminate. They are called greater in number because there are more vices than virtues. In the catalogue they are called seven nations, in the conquest they are put without number; but, when he shall have destroyed many nations before thee. For more numerous than Israel is the people of carnal passions, which is multiplied from the sevenfold tinder of vices. From gluttony come revelling and drunkenness; from fornication, foul speech, scurrility, jesting, and foolish talk; from avarice, lying, fraud, thefts, perjuries, desire of base gain, false witness, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity; from anger, murder, clamour and indignation; from sadness, rancour, faint-heartedness, bitterness, and despair, and sloth; from acedia, idleness, drowsiness, importunity, restlessness of mind and body, instability, wordiness, and curiosity; from vainglory, contentions, heresies, boasting, and presumption of novelties; from pride, contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many others. Although these are greater in number than the virtues, yet when the principal ones are conquered all fall quiet and are destroyed by perpetual death. That these plagues are stronger we feel in temptation: for the delight of carnal passions fights more strongly in our members than the pursuits of virtues, which are acquired by the utmost contrition of heart and body. We possess the regions of these nations with the army of Israel, that is, we overcome vices by virtues. So that in our heart chastity may hold the place of fornication; patience the place of fury; saving joy the place of sadness; fortitude dwell in the place of acedia; humility in the place of pride; thus, the individual vices being expelled, the children of Israel, that is, the souls seeing God, reign in their place. But when God spoke to Abraham of future things, he is read to have numbered not seven but ten nations, whose land is promised to his seed, namely the idolatries of the Gentiles, the blasphemy of the Jews, the error of heretics, to which they are subject, who before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism dwell in the spiritual Egypt. But he who goes out from there and by the grace of God comes to the spiritual wilderness is freed from the assault of three nations and engages against seven. The Hittite and the Girgashite, etc. JEROME, On Hebrew Names, vol. 3. Hittite, etc., until that is, trodden down, or their manger. Seven nations. It was permitted to Abraham that ten be destroyed: for then there were ten, but when the children of Israel crossed to the Jordan, three had already been destroyed. For the children of Lot destroyed the giants; the children of Esau the Horites; and the Cappadocians part of the Hivites. And stronger. Spiritual wickednesses are subtler, and have more power to deceive than the weakness of men has to endure.
7.14: 7.14 Barren. There were some barren women among the Jews, but so few that in comparison with the fruitful ones they seemed none.
7.20: 7.20 Moreover also the hornets, etc. It is not read anywhere in the history that God sent hornets or wasps against their enemies. But through stinging animals he designates the pricks of fear, by which he put the terrified enemies to flight.
7.22: 7.22 Thou canst not, etc. He shows that we must be careful lest, sins having been driven from our flesh, a spiritual beast rise up, that is, boasting, pride, or vainglory, which are more difficult to root out than carnal vices. For Lot, who was continent in Sodom, was defiled by fornication on the mountain (Genesis 19). When a vice is expelled, let a virtue immediately be planted, lest the unclean spirit return and find the house empty (Matthew 12). RABANUS, GREGORY. To some God gives greater goods, and does not grant lesser ones, so that their mind may always have something for which to blame itself, and while they desire to be perfect and cannot, they may in no way exalt themselves over what they have, who of themselves cannot have even small things. Hence it is that he destroyed the strong and powerful adversaries, the Philistines; and long preserved the Canaanites, that Israel might be trained in them, having someone to fight against, lest it exalt itself over the greater ones defeated. The same mind, therefore, is strong from virtue and grows weak from infirmity, so that while it seeks what it cannot have, it may humbly keep what it has. The heavenly region also suffered loss in part of its citizens and in part stood firm: so that the elect angels, seeing others fall through pride, might stand all the more strongly the more humbly. So it goes in each soul: things that bring the greatest gains sometimes cause the least losses.
7.26: 7.26 Anathema, that is, from setting up on high, or hanging up, as votive offerings were hung up in temples, and were set apart from those who gave them.
8.2: 8.2 Forty years. For therefore he permitted them to be afflicted for forty years, that they might know how great their frailty was. To afflict thee. AUGUSTINE, question 13. Here it is said more openly, etc., until for if he had said so, it would have had to be understood as: he would make known.
8.3: 8.3 Manna. The flesh of Christ, by which, refreshed, we may come to the true land of promise. Forty years we eat manna, that is, in all our time, which turns on four seasons, we are fed by the sacrament of the Lord's body. Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every, etc. Spiritual food is commended, by which souls destined to live for ever are satisfied. The manna given from heaven signifies the flesh of Christ, who says: I am the bread of life, this is the bread that came down from heaven (John 6), because the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. He who eats this flesh has eternal life. Not in bread alone, etc. It signifies the twofold substance of our nature. For man consists of soul and body: the body, which is from the earth, is nourished with earthly food; the soul, however, lives by the word of God; and the Spirit of God gives life to the spirit of man, provided man is in the body of the Church, that is, of Christ, and in the faith of the Son of God. Therefore he adds: Thy garment did not decay with age; because the way of life of the new man must remain in newness of life, whose foot is not worn, because the steps of his works are kept unharmed: For the Lord knoweth the way of the just, and the way of the wicked shall perish (Psalm 1).
8.11: 8.11 Judgments. Those which were commanded to the people through Moses at various times after the giving of the law, which in Exodus are called justifications. And ceremonies. Circumcision, the rites of sacrifices. Hence Ambrose on the Epistle to the Romans: He says the law is threefold: the first part concerns the sacrament of the divinity; the second agrees with the natural law, which forbids sin; the third is that of the feasts of the law, that is, the sabbaths, the new moons, and circumcision.
8.15: 8.15 And the dipsas. A kind of asp which in Latin is called situla; whomever it bites perishes of thirst; so small that when it is trodden on it is not seen. Its venom kills before it is felt, and the one about to die feels no sadness. Mystically: the various serpents are heresies, different from one another indeed, but all deadly.
9.5: 9.5 For neither, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 14. These are they who did not deserve to perish in the desert, etc., until where they provoked the Lord, who by their own merit were not brought into the promised land.
9.10: 9.10 And he gave, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 15. In Exodus it is read that the Lord gave the tables to Moses, etc., until endures for ever.
10.4: 10.4 And he wrote on. AUGUSTINE, question 14 on Deuteronomy. In Exodus Moses, etc., until but he himself assists the choice of a good will.
10.6: 10.6 In Mosera, etc. In the book of Numbers he is written to have died on Mount Hor, but perhaps the place has two names. For Beeroth of the sons of Jaakan is a place in the desert, like Moserah, where Aaron died, as is read in the books on places. And it is shown to this day at the tenth milestone from the city of Petra on the summit of a mountain.
10.8: 10.8 The tribe of Levi. Unless the whole royal priesthood, which belongs to the New Testament, were signified by this, a man who was not of that tribe would not dare to say: The Lord is my portion (Psalm 72); and elsewhere: The Lord is the portion of my inheritance, etc. (Psalm 15).
10.14: 10.14 The heaven of heaven, etc. Some say there are three heavens, the aerial, the ethereal, and the starry. Some say seven: the first aerial, the second ethereal, the third Olympian, the fourth fiery, the fifth the firmament, the sixth watery, the seventh of the angels.
10.16: 10.16 Circumcise, etc. He signifies spiritual circumcision, that is, the guarding of the mind and true abstinence. As if to say: when you have extinguished the lust of the flesh, cut away also the superfluities of the mind. All the senses must be circumcised. Hence Moses complains of being uncircumcised in lips; and Stephen says to the Jews: Uncircumcised in heart and ears, etc. (Acts 7). Truly circumcised, then, is he who stops his ears lest he hear of blood, and closes his eyes lest he see evil; who does not offend with his tongue, whose heart is not weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness, who washes his hands among the innocent, and keeps his feet from every evil way; who chastises his body and brings it into subjection, and keeps his heart with all custody. We also need a double circumcision, lest we seek vain glory from these things, lest we be clean outside and unclean within, and bear the penalties of feigned holiness, like the Shechemites who imitated the circumcision of the patriarchs not out of love of God but for the sake of lust: therefore they gained no reward, but on the third day perished within the ruins of their city. For such persons at the time of the resurrection, the virtues in which they trusted being emptied out, die for ever.
10.22: 10.22 Thy fathers went down into Egypt. One goes down into Egypt: easy is the descent to Avernus. One goes up to Jerusalem, because narrow is the way that leads to life, and virtue strives toward steep heights.
11.10: 11.10 From which thou camest out. In mind, with Moses as leader, that is, the law teaching to despise earthly pleasures, and entering the promised land with Jesus as leader. Of gardens. Because all carnal people desire to multiply for themselves present happiness and abundance of temporal things.
11.12: 11.12 From the beginning of the year. From the beginning, namely, of good will up to the perfection of the good work, he directs the course of life. For it is God who worketh in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will (Philippians 2).
11.14: 11.14 The early rain, etc. Because to his elect in the earlier time he conferred understanding of the law; he gives the latter rain, because in the last time he revealed to us the mystery of his incarnation. And the latter rain, etc. Because it is the last hour when his preaching reaches us, who says: The lifting up of my hands, an evening sacrifice (Psalm 140).
11.20: 11.20 Thou shalt write them upon the posts. AUGUSTINE, question 17. Is this according to the letter, or is it a hyperbolic commendation, as many things are said?
11.29: 11.29 Mount Gerizim. Gerizim is interpreted Division or Stranger; Ebal, Old Abyss. For those who separate themselves from vices and judge themselves strangers and pilgrims in this world also deserve the eternal blessing. But those who cast themselves into the abyss of the old life, serving carnal desires, will lie under the eternal curse.
12.6: 12.6 Tithes and firstfruits, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 18. It must be asked how he commands that the tithes of all fruits and the firstborn of all cattle not be eaten except in the city where the temple was, when in the law he commanded that they be given to the Levites.
12.13: 12.13 Beware lest thou offer. He cuts off the occasion of sacrificing to idols. For he therefore commands victims to be offered in the temple and at the altar of the Lord, so that where religion is whole, there fitting worship may be rendered. Mystically, however, he hints that no gift is acceptable to God outside the Catholic Church; for this is the place which God has chosen to put his name there and to dwell in it.
12.16: 12.16 Without eating. He forbids murder. Blood is put for the soul, because the seat of the soul, that is, of human life, is in the blood.
12.17: 12.17 In thy towns. That is, you shall not ascribe to your merits what you have received by divine generosity, but not to your own strength but to God, by whose gift you have had it (Galatians 6).
12.23: 12.23 Only beware of this. According to the letter the apostles commanded this: And in blood murder is forbidden, and hatred of brethren. For he that hateth his brother is a murderer (1 John 3). For their blood. Because there is something vital in the blood, and by it above all one lives in this flesh, which is diffused through all the veins: he calls it the soul, that is, the life of the body, which ends in death. Mystically, however, it is hinted that when carnal men depart from their former way of life and join us in the unity of faith and good works, we should not turn their errors to our own use; but pour them out, that is, assign them, once confessed, to earthly frailty and cast them away as unworthy of spiritual men.
13.1: 13.1 If there arise. He wishes it understood that things said by diviners not according to God, even if they come to pass, are not to be taken in such a way that the things they predict happen, nor does he show that what thus happens is beyond his power. But he adds why he permits it: namely to make known how much those serving them love God, not for him, who knows all things.
14.1: 14.1 You shall not cut yourselves. To this day many nations cut themselves at the funerals of the dead. Hence: Be not sorrowful, even as others who have no hope. To do these things belongs to those who despair of the resurrection. Nor shall you make. The hairs of your head are all numbered (Matthew 10), that is, thoughts, which ought not to be taken away from the honour of the head and offered to the devil, as some offer bodily hair to the devil.
14.3: 14.3 Eat not. They are unclean animals, but they express by signification the habits, namely, of men, and their acts and wills.
14.5: 14.5 The camelopard. Sprinkled with white spots, in head like a camel, in neck like a horse, in feet like a wild ox, in the rest a leopard: it is born in Ethiopia. Every animal that divides. The Church receives and incorporates into her members those who part the hoof, who know how to discern good and evil, and who ruminate, that is, meditate on the law day and night.
14.6: 14.6 That divides in two parts. That is, one who, receiving the two testaments, establishes himself with a firm step of justice and innocence.
14.7: 14.7 The camel. The Jew who strains out a gnat and swallows a camel, who ruminates the letter but does not have a cloven hoof, because he does not divide the letter from the spirit: these are the scribes and Pharisees. The hare. By the hedgehog and the hare he signifies the multitude of the Jews, for each animal is feeble and weak. Because they chew the cud. The Jews ruminate the words of the law, but do not divide the hoof, because they do not believe in the Father and the Son, nor receive the two testaments. Certain heretics, however, part the hoof, but do not ruminate the doctrine of truth in the mouth (Leviticus 11).
14.9: 14.9 These you shall eat of all that move in the waters. By these the Gentiles are understood, who are born again in the waters of baptism. Those that have fins. Meditating on the law of a sublime and heavenly life; because ignorance of the divine law had long been among the Gentiles, he adds fins and scales: for as fish are scaled and finned, so to those who have temporal ignorance there is quickly added knowledge of the sublime and heavenly life.
14.12: 14.12 And the griffin. A four-footed beast, like an eagle in head and wings, and a lion in the rest of its body; it abounds in the Hyperborean mountains and is most hostile to horses and men.
14.15: 14.15 The ostrich. Which is not lifted from the earth, but is entangled in worldly business. The owl. Which sees sharply by night and not by day. Like those who glory in knowledge of the law and do not grasp the light of the Gospel. The gull. Which flies like a bird and swims like a water creature, namely one who reveres circumcision and baptism. To such Paul says: If you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing (Galatians 5). The hawk, etc. Which seem tame, but are allied with the powerful and the greedy.
14.16: 14.16 The swan and the ibis. These are said to have long necks and to draw their food from the depth of the earth: but we ought to seek the bread that came down from heaven, and not be solicitous what we shall eat (John 6; Matthew 6).
14.17: 14.17 The night raven. Which creeps and works by night, signifying those who are devoted to the works of night, which are fornication, uncleanness, worship of idols and the like.
14.18: 14.18 The hoopoe. Which loves mourning. But the sorrow of the world worketh death: we ought rather to rejoice in the Lord, in all things to give thanks (2 Corinthians 7; 1 Thessalonians 5). The bat, etc. Which flies near the earth and walks on its wings. But our conversation ought to be in heaven (Philippians 3).
14.21: 14.21 But whatever. Mystically, the ecclesiastical man is commanded to keep himself in holiness and avoid every uncleanness of sin, and to allow the stranger, that is, the Gentile, to remain in his filth. To the stranger that is within thy gates. As if to say: leave unclean things to pagans and heretics. Hence in the Gospel the demons are permitted to go into the herd of swine (Matthew 8), and it is said: Let the dead bury their dead (Luke 9). In milk: with moderate disciplines, but rather austere ones, so that they may restore the bitter things for the sweet things they lost.
14.22: 14.22 The tenth. As if to say: the good things you do, do according to the precepts of the divine law, and set them apart for the Lord, so that you may do all things to his praise.
14.23: 14.23 The firstborn. That is, the beginnings of good work, which are to be tithed, that is, consecrated to the Lord.
14.24: 14.24 To carry. As if to say: those who are far from the perfection of the saints, and cannot ascend the summit of virtues, nor be free for contemplation, let them do what they can, humbly and devoutly, and make themselves friends of the mammon of iniquity, and treasures in heaven, that they may be received into everlasting dwellings, where there will be feasting and rejoicing with friends, that is, the saints and elect of God.
14.26: 14.26 And thou shalt buy with the same money, etc. Spiritually it is commanded that we always persist in good works, so that after this life we may return to our house, that is, to the heavenly homeland.
14.28: 14.28 Another tithe. Besides that, namely, which you eat with your household and the Levites in the place which the Lord shall choose.
14.29: 14.29 And the Levite shall come. He clearly shows that this tithe is not to be shared with the one who offers it, but only with those to whom he commanded it to be distributed, among whom he placed the Levite in particular.
15.1: 15.1 In the seventh year. In this chapter piety and love are commended, that we may have mercy on our neighbours and expect reward from the Lord. For in due time we shall reap, not failing, if, while we have time, we work good to all men, but especially to those who are of the household of the faith (1 Timothy 5); whence: Forgive, and you shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given to you (Luke 6). In the seventh year. Because remission is in the sevenfold Spirit. Almost all the solemnities of the law are in the number seven: the sabbath is on the seventh day; Pentecost comes when seven weeks are finished; the seventh year too is celebrated; and the jubilee follows seven times seven years.
15.3: 15.3 From the stranger. Although all are our neighbours, mercy is to be shown above all to those who are members of Christ with us. For he that hath the substance of this world, and shall not give to his brother in need, how doth the charity of God abide in him? (1 John 3).
15.6: 15.6 Thou shalt lend. As if to say: you will be richer than all nations. The Church too abounds in spiritual riches: she teaches, and has no need to be taught.
15.9: 15.9 Beware. AUGUSTINE, question 21. The Septuagint: Take heed to thyself, lest there be a hidden word, etc., until if he thinks cruelly that it should not be given at the time when it ought to be given?
15.12: 15.12 When he shall have been sold to thee, etc. ISIDORE. If a Hebrew boy comes into slavery, etc., until namely we shall serve sins for ever. When he shall have been sold to thee, etc. The Hebrew, a passer-by, who is heading to the eternal homeland, and passes from vices to virtues, from earthly to heavenly things; if such a one sells himself to you, that is, has devoted himself to your mastery, you will teach him to strive in the present life to work, so that he may be able to come to rest. This is: six years he shall serve thee, in the seventh thou shalt let him go free, and shalt not suffer him to go away empty; as if to say: you will promise him eternal rewards and true freedom in the other life. But if he shall say, I will not go out, because he loves thee and thy house, that is, if the good things he has done he has done not for an eternal reward but for human praise, as one loving the present life, thou shalt bore through his ear with an awl, that is, his mind with the terror of judgment; thou shalt pierce it at the door of the house, because judgment will be at the going out of this life and the entering of the other, and he shall serve thee for ever, that is, you will teach him that if he has loved the world more than God, he is to be consigned to eternal torments. GREGORY, homily 3 on Ezekiel. Since the active and the contemplative life are ours by the grace of God, etc., until where the ear of one refusing freedom is commanded to be pierced with an awl.
15.16: 15.16 But if he shall have. There are some works which, though they please God less, nevertheless benefit the neighbour; and if they cannot be offered to God, they can be eaten. For though they please God less because of the dimmed intention which God beholds, yet they help neighbours by example. Like the roe and the stag. The roe goes by leaps, the stag is an enemy of the serpent, and leaping over rough and thorny places, climbs the mountains, and therefore they are taken in a good sense.
15.19: 15.19 Of the firstborn. AUGUSTINE, question 23. He says firstborn, etc., until because he alone is of the substance of the Father, and equal and coeternal. Thou shalt sanctify to the Lord thy God. Not to yourself, but to the giver of all: Every best gift is from above (James 1). But whatever is light in our thought, or spotted in our conduct, or lame in the progress of our works, or blind through ignorance of mind, or deformed or weak in any part, we ought not to offer to God, that is, impute to him, but to ourselves. Thou shalt not work. GREGORY, Morals, book 8, chapter 34. In the firstborn of the ox to plough, etc., until the deceived mind does not detect the evils that are in them.
16.1: 16.1 Observe the month of the new corn. Because in it the sheaves of ears, that is, the firstfruits, were offered to the Lord through the priest. The first month, namely of the Hebrews, which among them is called Nisan, among the Greeks too, and among the Latins April, in which the paschal lamb was slain. He brought thee out. Allegorically: let us also, freed from the Egypt of this world and clothed with the new man, walk in newness of life, consecrating the firstfruits of good works and celebrating the phase, that is, the good passage, so that, leaving Egypt, we may come to the promised land.
16.2: 16.2 And of oxen in the place. AUGUSTINE, question 24. He adds oxen, though he commanded only of the sheep, which he ordered to be taken from the sheep and kids or goats, either on account of Christ, who according to the flesh was of the just and of sinners. For he does not say from sheep or goats, but from sheep and goats, although strictly a sheep is not understood from goats, lest the Jews say that a he-goat is to be understood. Why then were oxen added? Is it on account of the other sacrifices which are to be offered in the days of the unleavened bread?
16.3: 16.3 Leavened bread. Corrupt doctrine or the old way of life, whence: Let us feast with the unleavened bread, not with the old leaven, etc. (1 Corinthians 5). Seven. The whole time of the present life. As they ate unleavened bread for seven days, so let us live purely and simply through the seven days of this life, in which daily the lamb is slain and the pasch is celebrated, if, made new, we retain nothing of the old corruption. For what else is leaven but the corruption of nature? What is leavened departs from its natural sweetness and is spoiled by an adulterate rancidity.
16.4: 16.4 It shall not appear. Let us feast not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, etc. (1 Corinthians 5), as if to say: put off the old man, and put on the new. Nothing shall remain. In this life all the sacraments of the Lord's incarnation are to be searched out, and all his commandments fulfilled (Ephesians 4), before the morning, that is, the end of the age, arrives.
16.5: 16.5 Thou mayest not. In one house the paschal lamb is eaten, and in one place the phase is sacrificed, that is, in the Catholic Church: outside it the pasch is not rightly celebrated. He forbids celebrating the mysteries of Christ in the conventicles of heretics.
16.6: 16.6 In the evening at the going down of the sun. In the last age of the world, when the true Sun set in the passion and loosed the Egyptian captivity, when Christ our pasch was sacrificed.
16.7: 16.7 Thou shalt go to thy tents. When the service of the Lord is completed, on the morning of the resurrection we shall pass into the eternal tabernacles, to rest from all labour, rejoicing in the reward received.
16.8: 16.8 On the seventh day. In the eternal rest, which the number seven signifies: on account of the sabbath, where there is no labour, no reason for working.
16.9: 16.9 Seven weeks. In Leviticus more fully: You shall count therefore from the morrow after the sabbath seven full weeks, until the morrow after the seventh week is ended. AUGUSTINE, question 25. Seven weeks, etc. If this Pentecost was commanded to be observed by the whole people, is it to be believed that all were ordered to put the sickle to the harvest on one day? But if each one observes this fiftieth day for himself, counting from the day on which he puts in the sickle, it is not one for the whole people. That one, however, is single which is reckoned from the sacrifice of the pasch to the day of the giving of the law on Sinai. We too celebrate Pentecost, that is, the coming of the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, by which the law was written on tablets.
16.13: 16.13 The solemnity. He who uses the present world as a tabernacle can keep festival and rejoice in it, because of the expectation of the future: For if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, we have a house not made with hands in heaven (1 Corinthians 5). When. It signifies that, the perfection of all good things being completed and many virtues gathered together, there is to be rejoicing and exultation with friends. When each one who has been generous here in giving exults in the reward received, then truly the solemnity of tabernacles will be kept, not of changeable ones but of eternal ones; whence: That they may receive you into everlasting dwellings (Luke 16).
16.16: 16.16 The male. Not the female; for there ought to be nothing soft, fragile, or weak in our way of life: God demands from us all strong things (Exodus 23, 34; Ecclesiasticus 35). But if in the faith of the Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with a view to the eternal reward, we toil in the time of this present life at good works, we set up a male in the sight of the Lord. In all. So that those coming from every side may at once at the entrance find ready those from whom they may receive just judgments.
16.19: 16.19 The eyes of the wise. Before men, not before God; to whom it is said: Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes (Isaiah 5).
16.20: 16.20 Justly. GREGORY, Morals, book 10, chapter 19. He pursues what is just unjustly who is stirred to defend justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of temporal reward, and is not afraid to sell the justice which he puts forward. To pursue what is just justly is therefore, in asserting justice, to seek justice itself: There are ways that seem just to men, etc. (Proverbs 14). And: Woe to you who justify yourselves before men (Luke 16).
16.21: 16.21 Thou shalt not plant. He cuts off the occasion of idolatry. For the nations were accustomed to sacrifice, and to adore statues in shrines. A grove. ISIDORE. A grove, leafy unfruitful trees, etc., until nor does he permit the fiction of falsehood or error to be joined to Catholic truth.
17.2: 17.2 And when there shall be found.
