The law especially detests error and idolatry: for it is the greatest crime to give the honour of the Creator to the creature; which the Gentiles do, and bad Catholics, who, though they do not leave the Church, are nevertheless found to serve the devil through various vices rather than to fight for God through good works. These he orders to be overwhelmed with stones, whom the irrevocable sentence foresaw must be condemned.
17.6: 17.6 At the mouth of two or three witnesses. Namely by the testimony of the law, the prophets and the Gospel, according to that: The word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day (John 12). On the title of the cross also three languages testify that Christ is king of the Jews: Hebrew, Greek and Latin (John 19). Let no man be put to death. There is such concord between the Old and New Testaments that neither exists without the other. In human judgment the authority of the divine Scripture is first to be sought.
17.8: 17.8 If there be a hard matter. He instructs the priests of the Church of God to conduct ecclesiastical judgments reverently according to the power given them by God, and to decide justly, not at their own pleasure but according to the decree of the law, lest by accepting a person they change the sentence.
17.11: 17.11 According to. Note, it is not said to you to obey unless they teach according to the law, whence: The scribes and the Pharisees have sitten on the chair of Moses (Matthew 23).
17.12: 17.12 The command of the priest. Of Christ, who is a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech, who appointed vicars in his place, to whom he says: He that heareth you, heareth me; and he that despiseth you, despiseth me, etc. (Luke 10). By the right of condemnation, therefore, he bears the sentence who despises the power of the divinity.
17.14: 17.14 When thou art come into the land, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 26. It may be asked why the people displeased God when they desired a king, since in this passage it is found to have been permitted. But it must be understood that it was deservedly not according to the will of God, because he did not command this to be done, but permitted it to those who desired it. Yet he commanded that it should not be a stranger, but a brother from the same people, a native and not a foreigner. As for what he says: Thou mayest not, it is to be understood as: thou shalt not be allowed. I will set over me. The inhabitants of the land set up a king for themselves against the judgment of God.
17.17: 17.17 He shall not have, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 27. It is manifest that Solomon transgressed this precept, etc., until it comes to foreigners. Nor silver. Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth (Matthew 6).
17.19: 17.19 And he shall read. Note with what assiduity priests ought to read, since kings read assiduously. Reading itself is light and life, whence: The words that I speak to you, are spirit and life (John 6).
17.20: 17.20 Pride. As if to say, let him know that he is a brother. We all have one Father, God, to whom we say: Our Father, who art in heaven, etc. (Luke 11). Pride. It is a blessing to reign over Israel, namely by reigning to make Israel, namely those seeing God.
18.1: 18.1 They shall not have. Both in the Old and in the New Testament the ministers of the altar are commanded to live from oblations and tithes, and it is not granted them to long for acquiring earthly possessions: whence: Do not possess gold nor silver, etc. (Matthew 10); and after a few lines: The workman is worthy of his meat (1 Corinthians 9). And elsewhere: They that serve the altar partake with the altar (Numbers 18). For it is not fitting that he who must always stand at the divine office should long for earthly gain, he whose inheritance is God. What, then, can be lacking to him who has him who has all things?
18.2: 18.2 The inheritance. For good work, that what he has conceived in mind he may prove in deed, whence: Jesus began to do and to teach (Acts 1).
18.3: 18.3 They shall give. Because we ought devoutly to share with our teachers in bodily comforts and spiritual profits, whence: Let him that is instructed in the word communicate to him that instructeth him, in all good things (Galatians 6). The stomach. The belly is the receptacle of food; all the labours of men and the momentary enticements of the throat are for it, and he condemns their end: and to minds consecrated to God he shows that all we devour is cast out in the end, whence: Meats for the belly, and the belly for the meats: but God shall destroy both it and them.
18.4: 18.4 The firstfruits. The labouring husbandman ought first to receive of the fruits the firstfruits of the crops.
18.6: 18.6 If he come. As if he leaves city and home, who serves God freely and sets forth the Gospel without charge.
18.8: 18.8 Except. AUGUSTINE, question 38. What the Septuagint, etc., until what was shown to the parents ought to be preserved for him.
18.9: 18.9 When thou art come in. AUGUSTINE, question 29. Since inspectors of portents are forbidden, etc., until so those inspections of prodigies are to be distinguished from the signification of miracles.
18.10: 18.10 Soothsayers. Who go around altars with unspeakable prayers and seek divination in the entrails of animals. Augury. As if avigeria, because they are carried out in the cries of birds. Or avigaria, from the chattering of birds.
18.11: 18.11 Pythons. Ventriloquists, from whose belly demons speak, so called from Python, that is, Apollo, whom they believed to be the god of divination.
18.15: 18.15 A prophet of. Although historically it can be taken of the prophets who after Moses in the people of Israel were filled with the Spirit of God, it is better taken of the Lord of the prophets, of whom the crowds, satisfied by him, said: This is of a truth the prophet that is to come into the world (John 6). And elsewhere: A great prophet is risen up among us (Luke 7).
19.2: 19.2 Three. Faith, hope and charity, to which all penitents ought to flee. Moses established three cities of refuge beyond the Jordan for homicides who committed homicide unwillingly, and commands another three to be set apart near the Jordan (Numbers 35; Joshua 20), mystically hinting that before receiving baptism, whoever wishes to be saved from sin and freed from spiritual enemies ought to confess faith in the holy Trinity with a sincere mind, and after baptism to work manfully in faith, hope and charity. And so, living religiously in the world, which was made in the number six, after the perfection of good works he awaits eternal rest in the sabbath-rest.
19.3: 19.3 Into three. So that he who is to be saved may escape more easily. Preachers also ought by word and example to take counsel for sinners, and equally in the whole land of the Church to make known to all the faith of the Trinity, that they may recognize that the way of truth and the gate of faith lie open to them, and that they deservedly will be condemned if they refuse to enter. But gone. For by the example he shows what sort of homicide is to be saved. GREGORY, Pastoral Rule, part 2, chapter 10, vol. 3. We go to the wood with a friend, etc., until which is not committed maliciously. AMBROSE, On Flight from the World, chapter 2. It is evident that provision was fittingly made, etc., until struck by the Levitical sword, let the sense of the flesh die, that your soul may live.
19.9: 19.9 Thou shalt add to thee. In the book of Joshua six cities of refuge are appointed for such homicides (Joshua 20): Kedesh in Galilee of Mount Naphtali, Shechem in Mount Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, in Mount Judah. And beyond the Jordan, Bezer of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan of the tribe of Manasseh. AMBROSE, as above. The refuges are of six cities, etc., until or let us reverence by turning away from things forbidden.
19.11: 19.11 But if any man, hating his neighbour. Whoever strikes anyone out of malice and leads him to the death of the soul is guilty of eternal death, whence: Whosoever shall scandalize one of these little ones that believe in me, etc. And elsewhere: He that hateth his brother is a murderer, and shall not have eternal life (Matthew 18; 1 John 3). This man is torn from the altar as unworthy of the Lord's sacraments, and obtains pardon only through fitting penance. But he who kills unwillingly has cities of refuge, namely the Catholic Church, where, restraining himself in the narrowness of penance, he strives for the whole time of this present life in good works, and if he places his hope in the death of the high priest, namely of his Redeemer, he will at last deserve to be saved. He who retains hatred of his brother in his heart cannot do fruitful penance, nor appease God.
19.14: 19.14 Thou shalt not take away and remove the landmarks, etc. Whence: Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set (Proverbs 22), that is, the rules and definitions of living of the fathers who have gone before.
19.15: 19.15 One witness shall not stand. We ought to observe this historically also. And against the wicked or heretics, when we need testimonies of the Scriptures, we bring two witnesses, that is, the Old and New Testament, or three, that is, the Gospel, the prophets and the apostle, and so the word stands.
19.21: 19.21 Life for life. For he who has made a soul err is not worthy of pardon. Tooth for tooth (Exodus 21; Leviticus 24; Matthew 5). The power of words. For teeth signify words, according to that: The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons (Psalm 56). And elsewhere: His teeth whiter than milk, that is, than the law (Genesis 29). Hand, etc. Operation, so that those things, namely, are useful or harmful to him which he perverts in another.
20.1: 20.1 For the Lord. Mystically. AUGUSTINE, question 30. The Septuagint: For the Lord, etc., until that he might show that they themselves would also act.
20.5: 20.5 What man is there. The same, question 31. He is not better in war who has already dedicated buildings, etc., until but these things were instituted to test the minds of the men. What man is there. ISIDORE. He teaches that no one can undertake the profession of contemplation or spiritual warfare, etc., until: that he may please him to whom he has engaged himself (2 Timothy 2). It is better to avoid the profession or the persecution than to succumb in it. Nor ought anyone to come to a disputation against heretics unless he is learned and perfect, lest being defeated he scandalize others.
20.16: 20.16 Thou shalt suffer none at all. No vice in our way of life is to be spared, lest before the eyes of the Lord we appear corrupted by pleasures and abominable, and our enemies, exulting over our ruin, say: Well, well, our soul is satisfied, we will devour him (Psalm 34).
21.1: 21.1 When there shall be found, etc. The corpse: a body without a soul, and a soul without God, who is its life. In the land which the Lord thy God will give thee, that is, in the Church. The guilty of the slaying: the author of sedition; the elders: greater in life and wisdom. The judges, that is, priests, whose office is to judge of individual things, that is, to discern. They shall measure from the place of the corpse, that is, with the highest discretion they will investigate the author of the sedition. They shall take a heifer out of the herd, that is, the flesh of Christ, which he took from the fathers. Which hath not drawn in the yoke, because he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. Nor cleft the earth with a ploughshare (1 Peter 2), namely he committed no stain of sedition. And the guilty of the slaying shall not be known. The devil, who is invisible and is therefore said to be unknown, though it is known that he put it into the heart of Judas to betray him (John 13). The elders, etc. The apostles and teachers, who have perceived by the testimony of Scripture that no nation is so ready for slaughter as the nation of the Jews, who shed both the blood of the prophets and of the Lord.
21.4: 21.4 And they shall bring her to a rough and stony valley, etc. Namely a despised and most shameful death, whence: Let us condemn him to a most shameful death. Which was never ploughed (Wisdom 2), because the death of Christ was without fault. Nor received seed (Matthew 13), that is, the cockle of sin, which the enemy man sowed over. We can understand by the rough valley the Gentile world, which was rough; stony, because it worshipped stones; in which the neck of the heifer was cut, because for the salvation of the Gentiles the death of Christ was celebrated. The neck: the strength of the flesh which he laid down in death. They shall wash their hands over the heifer, that is, they will cleanse their works through confidence in the passion of Christ.
21.6: 21.6 And they shall wash their hands, etc. That is, they will show their works to be clean in the passion of Christ. For although the sacraments of that same passion are repeated daily, yet they have hearts and works most clean from all deceit of the Jews.
21.8: 21.8 Be merciful. In their office they bless the people, that vengeance may not be rendered for the crime, but salvation for the redemption.
21.10: 21.10 If thou go out to fight. ISIDORE. Let the Jews say how they keep these things. What is the reason that the woman is shaved bald and her nails pared? What if she is found without hair and nails?
21.11: 21.11 A beautiful woman. As Paul, who took from Menander: Evil communications corrupt good manners (1 Corinthians 15). And from Aratus: In him we live, and move, and are: for we are also his offspring (Acts 17). Others think this woman, beautiful in form, signifies rational discipline found among the Gentiles: from it, indeed, all the uncleanness of superstition must be cut away, so that it may be taken up for the study of truth. For the disciplines of the Gentiles have nothing clean, because among them there is no discipline with which something of uncleanness or superstition is not mixed.
21.13: 21.13 For a month, that is, thirty days, so that after faith in the Trinity and the work of the law she may deserve to be joined to the Church; for three times ten make thirty. And afterwards. When there will be nothing superfluous or unclean either in the head, that is, in the senses, or in the hands, that is, in the works.
21.15: 21.15 If a man have two wives, etc. Christ joined to himself two wives, namely the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles, in the name of marriage. The synagogue is the hated one, always contentious, stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart; the Gentile Church is the beloved. But he cannot prefer the son of the beloved to the son of the hated, that is, prefer the Church from the Gentiles and her sons to the apostles and the other first ones, who are sons of the synagogue. He acknowledges the firstborn of the hated, gives him a double portion, because to the first sons of the synagogue he gave the law and the prophets, and knowledge of his name, and first preached the Gospel to them. For this is the firstborn of his children. One beloved. Animality, which seems sweet and delightful: it desires all pleasurable things and brings no sorrow. The other hated. Rationality, which does not indulge the body nor serve pleasure, but renounces the hidden things of shame.
21.16: 21.16 The firstborn. The apostles and apostolic men, who hold the place of the firstborn, whose authority the Church follows.
21.17: 21.17 But the son. This is to be done according to the letter, that one may follow not the impulse of his own mind, nor love, nor hatred, but nature. All double things. The apostles received all double things, being endowed with teaching and works. To the other he will give so that he may live, not so that he may abound, as Abraham set the son of the handmaid over nations: to the son of Sarah he heaped up not only temporal but spiritual things (Genesis 12).
21.18: 21.18 If a man beget. Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to hearken rather than to offer the fat of rams, for it is like the sin of witchcraft to rebel, etc. (1 Kings 15). Moses therefore commands a disobedient and vicious son to be overwhelmed with stones: the Gospel also rebukes such persons with hard reproofs, as if with stones: Ye brood of vipers, who hath shewed you to flee from the wrath to come? (Luke 3).
21.22: 21.22 Hanged. His torment being seen by the people, whence: Them that sin reprove before all, that the rest also may have fear (2 Timothy 5).
21.23: 21.23 Shall not remain. That is, he ought not to be left in the same condemnation, but recalled by the exhortation of teachers, so that to no one, while he lives, reconciliation may be denied. Shall not remain. Penance is not to be put off from day to day, but done at once, so that through fruitful penance offences may be hidden from the eyes of God, whence: Blessed are they whose sins are covered (Psalm 31). Accursed of God. AUGUSTINE, Against Faustus, book 14. Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us (Galatians 3). For Adam fell on the tree of transgression: therefore he deserved a curse for himself and his descendants, of which it says: Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. And he took on a cursed, that is, execrable and most shameful, death. The same, as above, chapters 3, 4. Accursed of God is he that hangeth, etc. Certain heretics transfer this sentence to slander the passion of Christ, etc., until it is therefore rightly called a curse, because what God hates hung on the tree. Thou shalt defile. We ought to wash away the stench of sins with the tears of penance, lest it cause scandal to others and torment to ourselves.
22.1: 22.1 Thou shalt not see. Morally: your brother, a teacher of the Church, whose disciple, either learned, who is signified by the ox, or unlearned, who is signified by the sheep, if you see him go astray, do not neglect him, but exhort him as a brother, that is, so that you may be able to reconcile him with the master. Bring them to thy house (1 Corinthians 11), that is, give care. And if he be not near, that is, of your Church, but a teacher of another.
22.3: 22.3 In like manner. Of the Gentile, namely, whose usefulness and uncleanness we ought not to despise. Garment. The people with which the teacher is adorned. According to the letter also all these and similar things are to be observed.
22.5: 22.5 A woman shall not be clothed, etc. AUGUSTINE, question 32. Another edition, etc., until ought not to have anything feminine or soft in his teaching. Woman. Whose colour is naturally different, movement unchaste, strength; who is not permitted to teach, nor to have dominion over a man, nor to usurp the office of preaching (1 Corinthians 13). It is against nature for a man to do womanly things, to curl the hair, to twist the locks, whence the Apostle: If a man nourish his hair, it is a shame unto him. But to a woman her hair is given for a covering; a man therefore shall not be clothed with a woman's garment, namely with loose and dissolute behaviour. RABANUS. We go by the road, etc., until but from it we retain the allegorical sense in the mind.
22.8: 22.8 A new house, that is, the Church. A battlement for the roof, that is, the guarding of virtues. That blood be not shed in thy house, that is, lest through another's sinning you be held guilty. GREGORY, Morals, book 8, chapter 39. That it be not shed. Through carelessness and sloth. Hence he who gathers virtues without humility carries dust, as it were, into the wind.
22.9: 22.9 Vineyard: doctrine, or the people entrusted to teachers, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to abound. With another seed, that is, heretical. The good seed is the word of God; the wicked seed is what the enemy sowed (Matthew 13): we must therefore take care that nothing of error be mixed in and the seed of God corrupted.
22.10: 22.10 Thou shalt not plough. ISIDORE. He ploughs with the ox and the ass who receives the Gospels with the observance of the Jews, which preceded in shadow. In the ox also is the life of those who work well, in the ass the sluggishness of fools: as if to say, do not join the foolish with the wise in preaching, lest through one who cannot fulfil the matter you hinder the one who prevails. But the foolish and the wise are rightly joined, so that one commands and the other obeys, not that they should announce the word of God with equal authority. Allegorically, he mixes wool or purple with linen garments who lives disorderly, and in progress of different kinds, as if a nun should have the ornaments of a wife, or a wife should assume the appearance of a virgin. What was figured in garments is now declared in conduct.
22.12: 22.12 Cords. For distinction, namely, as the sign of circumcision separates the Israelites from the rest. But superstitious masters, courting the favour of the people and gain from little women, enlarged their fringes and attached thorns to them, so that whether walking or sitting they might be pricked, and so be reminded to serve God, whence: They enlarge their phylacteries and make long their fringes.
22.13: 22.13 If a man take. AUGUSTINE, question 33. It appears how women subject to their husbands, etc., until by which the other was to be punished.
22.15: 22.15 His father and mother. The teachers of the Church, who like father and mother cherish the people: fathers by authority, mothers by piety.
22.18: 22.18 And they shall scourge. It is no wonder that a man who falsely accuses is commanded to be beaten and to pay a fine, but the girl, if guilty, to be stoned: because through woman was the beginning of sin, who seduced the man and sinned doubly, first against God, then against the man, while the man sinned only against God.
22.19: 22.19 A hundred sicles, etc. By the perfection of doctrine and the solicitude which he should bestow on the people subject to him, or of penance. For a hundred is perfect, fifty consecrated to penance.
22.23: 22.23 If a man find a damsel that is a virgin espoused. In this chapter, as in the two preceding and the two following, he condemns bodily fornication.
22.26: 22.26 She shall suffer nothing. But she will be recalled to the faith she began, freed from her enemies by the grace of baptism.
22.29: 22.29 He may not. AUGUSTINE, question 34. It is rightly asked whether this is the penalty, that he may not put away for all time her whom he disorderly and unlawfully violated; for if we understand that he cannot, that is, ought not, put her away for all time, because she has become his wife, there arises the fact that Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be given and her to be put away. In the case of those who unlawfully corrupt, however, he did not wish it to be permitted, lest he seem to have done it for sport and rather to have pretended that he had taken her. He also commanded this concerning her against whom the husband had slanderously claimed that the signs of virginity were not found.
22.30: 22.30 Not. Our Father is Christ, whose wife is the Church; it is not lawful for a man to transfer the dignity of this Bridegroom to himself, nor to violate his bride, so as to turn her love to himself, seeking his own praise and not God's from the gift of virtues or from preaching; to whom it is fitting to say: Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to thy name give glory (Psalm 103).
